# Working in Ocean

Local-first Node.js runtime for headless AI agents (Claude, Codex, Gemini, Hermes,
Antigravity). Public, provider-neutral engine; private data lives outside it.

## Commands

```bash
pnpm install          # deps
pnpm build            # tsc
pnpm test             # build + node --test tests/*.test.mjs
pnpm typecheck        # tsc --noEmit
pnpm check:style      # biome check .
```

## Hard rules

- No credentials, no personal data — anywhere in source, config, logs, tests, docs.
- Public code only under `packages/*/src/`. Provider execution only under
  `packages/harness/src/infrastructure/providers/`.
- Private personal/project data (`brain/`) lives as a sibling of this repo, outside it
  entirely. Machine-local state (`bridge/` — profiles, sessions, config, registry,
  integrations, archive) is physically nested inside this repo but git-ignored; never
  commit any of it.
- `sessions/sessions.sqlite` holds session metadata/events/links only — nothing else.
- Never add: `Adapters`, `Handoff`, `Mission`, `Coordinator`, the legacy Python/Bash
  runtime, hosted services, Postgres, Redis, dashboards.
- Never touch `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/`, `.gemini/`, `.claude/settings.json`, or any
  `pnpm-lock.yaml` entry without asking first.

## Cut tokens before reading code

1. When `graft` is installed and its graph is built (`graft build` creates the git-ignored
   `graft/`), `graft ask "<question>" --source` first — never grep or open files cold.
   Without it, search narrowly (`git grep`, a glob) instead of reading whole files.
   Full tool set: `packages/harness/skills/core/graft/SKILL.md`.
2. `catch-up` skill before touching anything you didn't just finish.
3. `core-thinking` before executing; smallest valid solution, not the biggest.
4. `verification` after — a claim isn't done until it's independently checked.
5. `session-handoff` when done — compact packet, not a transcript.

Headless prompts carry references, not bodies: a skill index with SKILL.md paths, a compact
profile contract, a facts digest (<= 2 KB, with a pointer) and context references (paths + why),
assembled in `packages/loop/src/runs/prompt-assembly.ts` and
`packages/context/src/context/context-references.ts`. `ocean context cost` reports each
client's always-on bytes (rules, memory index, skill frontmatter).

The section below applies only on a machine where `graft` is installed (`command -v graft`).

## Graft — repo context graph

This repo is indexed in `graft/`: small linked markdown nodes that explain each
system and carry exact file:line spans, kept in sync with the code through git.

For ANY task here — understanding how something works, finding where code lives,
or scoping a change — get context from the graph before grepping or opening
source files. Re-ask freely (it's cheap) and reuse literal identifiers you
already have (symbol, error string, file name) as the query. New to this repo?
Run `graft map` first — a token-budgeted orientation (dir clusters, hubs,
hotspots), no LLM, no key.

- Run `graft ask "<your question>" --source` → ranked nodes with the relevant
  code spans inlined (each hit's ≤8-line crux by default; `--full` for whole
  definitions when the crux isn't enough). Match the tool to the task shape:
  for understanding or editing, the top node IS the answer — cite its
  `covers:` file:line spans and edit straight from `--source`. For
  exhaustive tasks ("every occurrence / every caller of this pattern"), ranked
  results are top-N, not complete — run `graft grep "<literal>"` instead
  (exhaustive over indexed files, grouped by enclosing symbol), falling back
  to raw `grep -rn` only for unindexed files.
- `graft skeleton <file>` → every definition's signature + span, ~10× cheaper
  than reading the file; use it to skim an API surface.
- `graft callers <symbol>` gives precomputed, exact edges — who calls this.
  Add `--direction out` for what it calls, or `--depth N` to walk
  transitively for the full blast radius. For structural questions, skip
  ranking and use this directly.
- Or browse: `graft/INDEX.md` lists every node; follow the links.
- Monorepos and folders of multiple repos rank fairly across sub-projects —
  hits carry `[scope/]` labels naming which one they're from. Narrow with
  `graft ask "<task>" --in <scope>/` once you know where you're working.

If a returned span is truncated ("+N more lines"), open the file at that exact
range before finalizing. Only open source files when a node genuinely lacks a
needed detail, and then at the exact file:line the node points to — never
re-read whole files.

After big code changes, refresh the graph with `graft build` (deterministic,
no API key, $0).

# Daily harvest

The owner decided (2026-11-16) that Ocean files what it learns on its own. You do not ask him to
review each item. You decide where each fact belongs, write it there, and report what you did
with a way to undo it. Only a contradiction stops and waits for him.

## Where everything lives

- A session from any client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Gemini, …) is one record in
  `01-daily/sessions/YYYY-MM/`, its client in `provider`.
- A fact is filed by **topic, not by which AI said it**: `routing.json` maps its type to a folder
  (identity, preference, goal, education, career, project memory, decision, solution, discovery,
  …). Its frontmatter keeps where it came from: `origin: imported|harvested`, `source:
  <client>`, the date.
- Raw memory pulled from a client waits in `00-inbox/native/<client>/` until harvested, then
  moves to `00-inbox/archive/native/<client>/<YYYY-MM>/`.

## 1. The mechanical pass

`ocean rhythm --yes` runs it all with no model, each part once per period (the service runs it
at every session start and end, and hourly): the morning block of today's note, every day not yet
harvested plus today so far, the archive, last week's digest, last month's review.

The daily note has one shape: `## Today` and `## Brief` (morning, under the title), then the day's
account — `## Day summary` (sessions per client, decisions, fixes, lessons, captures), `## Open
loops` (every Next, `- [ ]`, carried each morning until ticked), `## Corrections`, `## Time` — and
last `## Notes`, which is the owner's and never written. Claude Desktop chats and long Claude Code
sessions are in it through the digest their fact capture returns in the same call.

Read the JSON of `ocean harvest --pending --yes` (or the day's note): that is your work list.

## 2. The judgement pass

Work through these in order. For every fact: search first (`ocean memory search`), then either
strengthen the record that holds it (merge into one current statement, fresh `updated` /
`last_verified`) or create the record where `routing.json` puts its type. Never duplicate.

1. **Candidates** (`ocean memory review list`): a duplicate of a record → reject; new and
   consistent → approve with `--type` (or `--to`), then merge cleanly (the memory-review skill's
   step 3); unsure what it means → leave it and list it in the report.
2. **Native memory** in `00-inbox/native/<client>/` and the files in `02-personal/imported/`:
   split each into facts, file each by topic with `origin: imported` and its client, then move the
   raw file to the archive. A project fact goes to that project's `memory/`.
3. **Legacy session records** (no Decisions / Learned sections): read a month at a time; pull out
   decisions, fixes and lessons; file them as above; add `harvested: <date>` to each record read.
4. **Corrections** in the day summaries: one the owner gave twice, or with "always" / "never",
   becomes a feedback record in `02-personal/work/` (rule, **Why:**, **How to apply:**). A rule
   for every client goes to the backlog as a charter change, not into the charter itself.
5. **The system itself**: an error recurring across sessions (`ocean telemetry --yes`); the same
   manual steps in three or more sessions → a backlog line `skill: <what it would do>`; a failure
   in `05-knowledge/failures/` with no linked solution → look for the fix in the sessions.
6. **Knowledge hygiene**: merge records that say the same thing; list decisions whose
   `last_verified` is over 90 days old; fix broken links; run `ocean memory sync --apply`.
7. **The owner's journey**: a study session (IELTS, Letspeak) adds to his study log; finished,
   notable work becomes a milestone (`status: done`); a project's state goes to its `memory/`.

**Stop and do not write** when a fact contradicts a record or one of his notes in `07-notes/`:
propose it with `contradicts` so it waits in `02-personal/CONFLICTS.md`. Never write a secret;
about other people, only what the work needs; never invent a detail.

## 3. Archive

Run `ocean harvest archive --yes`: harvested days older than 30 days leave `01-daily/` for
`01-daily/archive/<YYYY-MM>/` (notes) and `01-daily/sessions/archive/<YYYY-MM>/` (records, still
searched). Nothing is deleted.

## 4. Report

In the owner's language, short: days harvested, records created and strengthened (by folder),
facts filed from other AIs, corrections turned into rules, backlog lines added, what waits in
CONFLICTS.md, what moved to the archive, and `ocean harvest undo <date>` for any day he wants back.

# Design Thinking

Use before non-trivial implementation or open-ended work.

1. State the user outcome in one sentence.
2. Separate observed facts, constraints, assumptions, and unknowns.
3. Identify the smallest useful result and the people or systems it affects.
4. Compare viable approaches by correctness, risk, complexity, and reversibility.
5. Choose the smallest approach that meets the outcome.
6. Define the evidence that proves completion before execution.

Do not turn exploration into implementation without a clear outcome. Ask one focused question only when a missing choice materially changes the solution.

# graft

`graft/` holds a graph of this repo: small markdown nodes that each explain one
part in prose and name the exact `file:line` spans they cover, plus a wiring
graph of who-calls-what. Querying a node costs a few hundred tokens; rebuilding
that understanding by reading source costs thousands, and misses the edges.

Every command below is `$0`, needs no API key, and returns in under a second.
There are six of them. **Pick the one that fits the task, run it, act on the
answer; don't chain tools hoping for more. Most tasks need one call.**

## The tools

### 1 · `graft ask "<question>" --source`: locate + understand (the default)
Ranked retrieval over the graph, routed automatically between prose nodes and
the wiring graph, returning the top hits with exact `file:line`.
- `--source` inlines the code at each hit, the ≤8-line **crux** of each
  definition, so the result IS the code you need, no follow-up file read. Add
  `--full` only when the crux is too small to act on.
- `--in <path>` narrows to a subtree before ranking; `-n N` caps results (default 8).
- **Use it when** the question is conceptual or locational: "how does auth
  work", "where is rate-limiting handled", "what assembles the request pipeline".
- One ask usually answers. A genuinely multi-part question needs one ask per
  distinct sub-aspect, never the same question reworded. Few or weak hits mean
  switch tool (grep / skeleton / callers), don't re-ask.

### 2 · `graft grep "<pattern>"`: exhaustive find
Regex (or `--fixed` for a literal) over every indexed file, hits **grouped by
enclosing symbol** and ranked by coupling; it also reports files it couldn't read.
- **Use it when** you need every occurrence: all call sites, all uses of a
  constant, all providers. `ask` is ranked top-N and *will* miss instances;
  grep won't. One grep replaces a spray of asks.
- Search a **short symbol name or literal**, not a full guessed signature: an
  over-specific regex (`func (s *Server) GenerateHandler`) returns nothing even
  when the code is indexed. If a grep misses, **loosen it** (drop the receiver
  and signature, keep the bare name) and retry `graft grep` — do NOT switch to
  raw `grep -rn`, which is slower and unranked.
- `-i` case-insensitive; `--in <path>` scopes to a subtree. Raw `grep -rn` is
  only for files graft genuinely doesn't index (docs, configs, brand-new files).

### 3 · `graft skeleton <file>`: a file's API at a glance
Signatures-only view of one file (every function / method / type with its span)
in ~200 tokens, ~10x cheaper than reading the file.
- **Use it when** you need "what's in this file / what can I call here" before
  editing or wiring into it. One skeleton is the whole answer for a file; don't
  re-skeleton the same file, and don't skeleton every file `map` already named.

### 4 · `graft callers <symbol>`: the exact edges
Precomputed call/reference edges, not a text search. Symbol can be bare
(`Foo`), qualified (`Class.method`), or package-qualified (`pkg.Fn`).
- default `--direction in`: **who calls/references** this; run before you
  rename, delete, or change its signature.
- `--direction out`: **what this symbol itself calls/depends on** (the old `callees`).
- `--depth N`: walk transitively N hops for the **full blast radius** (the old
  `impact`); `--depth 2` is the usual "what breaks if I touch this".
- `--depth all`: the **entire connected closure** — every source reachable
  through the edges. Reach for this before a **refactor, rename, or any
  multi-file change**: it surfaces the sibling and downstream files (platform
  variants, a module you must split out) that a single-file edit would miss.

### 5 · `graft map`: orientation for an unfamiliar repo or area
A token-budgeted tour: directory clusters, per-directory hubs, and global
hotspots, straight from the wiring graph.
- **Use it when** you land in a repo cold or are asked for "the architecture".
  `map` alone is the answer: read the hub cards it names; do NOT then skeleton
  or ask your way through every subsystem it lists. `--max-dirs N` widens it.

### 6 · Lifecycle: `graft build` / `graft check`
Every tool above refreshes the graph itself before answering, so what those tools
return always describes the code as it is right now — including edits you just made
and have not committed. You do **not** need to run `build` after editing.

One caveat, if you `grep` the markdown under `graft/` directly: those cards are a
projection, rebuilt at the end of the turn rather than on each query, so after an edit
they can lag. The tools above never do — prefer them, and treat a card's spans as
stale if you have edited that file this turn.

`build` is for the LLM layer (`--deep` adds a concept map; skip unless asked);
`check` fails when `graft/` is stale, for CI.

## Scenarios: the shortest path through a coding task

| When you're… | Reach for | Calls |
|---|---|---|
| Onboarding / "explain this codebase" | `graft map`, then read the named hub cards | 1 |
| Understanding a flow ("how does X work") | `graft ask "<flow>" --source` | 1 |
| Finding where a change belongs | `graft ask "where is <behavior>" --source` | 1 |
| Editing a symbol you can already name | `graft grep "<symbol>"`, edit at the `file:line` (skip `ask` — you know where it is) | 1 |
| Renaming / deleting / changing a signature | `graft callers <sym> --depth 2` first | 1 |
| Refactor / multi-file change (before editing) | `graft callers <sym> --depth all` — map every connected file, don't stop at the first | 1 |
| "What does this depend on?" | `graft callers <sym> --direction out` | 1 |
| Finding every occurrence of a pattern | `graft grep "<literal>"` | 1 |
| "What's the API of this file?" | `graft skeleton <file>` | 1 |
| Debugging a failure in area X | `graft ask "<symptom>" --source`, then `callers` on the suspect | 1–2 |
| Judging a diff's risk before merge | `graft callers <changed sym> --depth 2` | 1 / symbol |
| Working inside one repo of a monorepo | add `--in <scope>/` to ask / grep / callers | n/a |

In a multi-repo workspace, graft ranks fairly so the biggest repo can't drown
the rest, and every hit carries a `[scope/]` label naming its sub-project; when
you already know where you're working, narrow with `graft ask "<task>" --in <scope>/`.

## Spend the fewest calls
- A node's `covers:` list already gives exact `file:line` for every symbol, so
  cite straight from it. The spans are generated from source and authoritative;
  don't re-open or re-grep files to "double-check".
- When the task already names the file or symbol to change, go straight there:
  `graft grep "<symbol>"` for the exact `file:line`, then edit. Reserve
  `graft ask` for when you don't yet know where the code lives — an `ask`
  round-trip is wasted on a target you can already name.
- Trust the answer and act. Reach for a second tool only when the first genuinely
  fell short: weak hits, a truncated span, or a need to be exhaustive.
- If graft names a path that isn't on disk, its index is ahead of your checkout
  (a branch switch or unpulled move). Don't read the missing file — `graft grep`
  the symbol to find where it lives now, or run `graft build` to refresh.

## Report what graft saved, every turn
Each retrieval tool **opens** its output with a `[graft] tokens saved ≈ N` line:
the estimated tokens that call saved versus reading the files it covers whole.
Whenever you used any graft tool in a turn, close your reply with a one-line
tally summing those numbers across every graft call you made, e.g.
`🌱 graft saved ~12,400 tokens this turn (3 calls)`. A call with no such line
(tiny files, where the pointers cost as much as the source) saved nothing, so
skip it. This is the per-turn figure; the statusline carries the running
session total.

Once a turn has been billed, each line also states what that call was worth in
dollars, at the rate this session is actually paying for input tokens — include
that total alongside the tokens, e.g. `🌱 graft saved ~12,400 tokens (~$0.04)
this turn`. When a line carries no dollar figure, report tokens alone rather
than pricing them yourself.

**Never pipe a graft command through `head`, `tail`, or `sed -n`.** Every tool
is already capped and states what it dropped; clipping it costs you hits you
asked for, and it silently drops the savings line the statusline's running
total is parsed from.

## When graft isn't enough
- Span truncated ("+N more lines"): open the file at that exact range.
- A node lacks a detail: ask a more specific question; only then read source at
  the exact `file:line`, never a whole file to rebuild understanding graft gives.
- You may also grep / ls / cat inside `graft/` directly (plain markdown;
  `graft/INDEX.md` indexes the nodes), but the tools above are faster and
  exhaustive where it matters, so reach for them first.

When the graft MCP server is connected, these are exposed as tools too:
`graft_find_code`, `graft_find_all`, `graft_file_api`, `graft_trace_calls` (with
`direction` / `depth`), `graft_repo_map`, `graft_check_freshness`. Use whichever surface is
available; the guidance is identical.

# Loop

Use when a task must continue across time or while the owner is unavailable.

Before starting, require a task id, profile, scope, finite budget, maximum iterations, retry policy, and success condition. Each iteration must:

1. Read the task state and latest checkpoint.
2. Do one bounded unit of work.
3. Verify the unit with a real check.
4. Write a concise checkpoint with the next action.
5. Stop on success, budget exhaustion, repeated failure, missing input, authentication, or a consequential action requiring approval.

Never loop blindly over irreversible actions. Preserve the session and task state so a later run resumes from the checkpoint. Report completed work, evidence, remaining work, and the stop reason.

name: memory-review
description: Review pending memory candidates with the owner one at a time - compare each with the record it would change, recommend, and merge approved facts cleanly into that record. Use when he says review candidates, review my memory, go through the proposals, or clear the inbox candidates.

# Memory review

Candidates are facts Ocean proposed (inferred, imported or harvested). None is memory until the
owner approves it. You prepare each decision; he makes it.

## 1. Survey

Run `ocean memory review list`. Before asking anything, group what you see:

- **Duplicates**: the same source harvested twice (same `harvested from` path, same text). Decide
  them once, together.
- **Already recorded**: read the target record (or search with `ocean memory search <q>`). A
  candidate that adds nothing new is a reject to recommend, not a question to ask blind.
- **Age**: oldest first. Tell him the total and how many are older than seven days.

## 2. One candidate at a time

For each, read the candidate file and the record it would change. Show, in plain words in his
language:

1. **Now**: what the record says today (or that there is none).
2. **Proposed**: what the candidate adds or changes, with its source and date.
3. **Recommendation**: approve, merge, reject, or ask, with one line of why. Flag what may be
   stale ("as of October; still true?").

Then ask one question and wait. Never approve without his answer; never batch items he has not
seen.

## 3. Apply his answer

- **Approve, no target**: `ocean memory review approve <id> --type <type>` (`routing.json` picks
  the folder) or `--to <path>`. A project fact goes to that project's `memory/`.
- **Approve, existing record**: `ocean memory review approve <id>` appends the candidate's text
  to the record. Then merge by hand: fold the new facts into the right lines, delete what they
  replace, remove the appended raw paragraph, keep the frontmatter flat and set `updated` and
  `last_verified` to today. The record must read as one current statement, not a log.
- **Edit**: write his corrected version into the record, then reject the candidate.
- **Reject**: `ocean memory review reject <id>`.
- **His extra answers** (a date, "I cancelled that") go into the record too, dated.

Show him the few lines that changed after each one; nothing else.

## 4. Close

Run `ocean memory doctor` and report the count still waiting. Never write secrets, never record
facts about third parties beyond what work needs, and never invent a detail he did not give.

# Use Browser

Use when the user gives a URL and asks the agent to complete, fill, test, submit, or otherwise operate the page.

The skill defines the task and verification contract. When the user asks for their own
signed-in Chrome, the routes are in `docs/browser-clients.md`: the marketplace
`dev.ocean/chrome-devtools` entry (wired into every client by `ocean clients apply`), or Playwright MCP.
Ocean's `ocean browser` capability remains the deterministic local backend for repeatable
JSON task files.

Use Ocean's `ocean browser` capability through the terminal as the default browser backend. Do not switch to `claude-in-chrome`, an extension, or another browser connector unless the user explicitly asks for that backend. If Ocean cannot detect or open a browser, report the exact command result and stop; do not ask the user to install a different browser extension as the first workaround.

## Cost-aware execution

Keep browser work bounded and token-efficient. Use one `observe` and one targeted `read` before acting, prefer `extract` over rereading the whole page, and keep page text bounded. Do not run exploratory shell scripts or repeated reload/undo cycles when a deterministic browser operation is unavailable. Use at most one retry for a reversible step and no automatic retry for submit, upload, purchase, message, or other consequential actions. If the live state is ambiguous after the bounded attempt, stop and report the blocker instead of spending more tokens guessing.

## Workflow

1. Treat the URL as the starting location, not as permission to perform every possible action on the site.
2. Open or reconnect to an Ocean browser session with a persistent profile. Navigate to the URL.
3. Inspect the live page with `observe`, `read`, and targeted `extract`. Identify the page's current state, the user's intended outcome, required fields, available controls, and a concrete success signal.
4. Build the smallest step sequence that reaches the requested outcome. Prefer stable labels, roles, names, ids, and visible text. Use editor selectors for `contenteditable`, CodeMirror/Monaco containers, and `frame >>> editor` for same-origin iframe editors.
5. For code-editor changes, use `ocean browser replace-text <session-id> <selector> <old-text> <new-text> --occurrence <n>` when replacing a specific token. Never simulate a precise replacement by clicking and typing into the middle of a Monaco/CodeMirror line. Verify the returned editor value and then re-read the page.
6. Execute through Ocean browser operations or a bounded browser task file. Keep the task file small, cap retries at 0–1, and cap total steps to the minimum needed. After every state-changing step, verify the live post-condition. Stop if the page state contradicts the plan.
7. For forms, tests, purchases, uploads, messages, or other externally visible mutations, keep the existing Ocean approval gate. Ask for confirmation only at the final consequential action when approval is not already present.
8. If a field is ambiguous, required data is missing, authentication is needed, or the page reports failure, stop with the exact blocker. Do not invent personal, financial, legal, academic, or credential data.
9. Report the outcome, the verified success signal, and any unverified or blocked step. Close the browser session only if the user requested cleanup; otherwise preserve it for continuation.

## Client-neutral task prompt

Normalize browser requests to:

```text
url: <starting URL>
task: <human-readable outcome>
continue: true
verify: <observable success signal>
```

Use one bounded loop, verify every state-changing action, and stop when the
success signal is present or a required human decision is reached.

## Ocean execution shape

Use the browser capability's session lifecycle and task runner:

```text
ocean browser detect
ocean browser open --profile <profile>
ocean browser approve <session-id>
ocean browser navigate <session-id> <URL> --approve
ocean browser observe <session-id>
ocean browser read <session-id>
ocean browser replace-text <session-id> <selector> <old-text> <new-text> --occurrence <n>
ocean browser run <session-id> <task-file> --approve
```

Use direct operations for discovery and a bounded JSON task for repeatable execution. Keep task files small, set `retries` to 0–2, and never use retries to repeat an irreversible action blindly. The runner caps retries at three and stops on failed verification.

## Completion contract

A task is complete only when the requested outcome is visible in live page state: a success message, changed status, expected navigation, submitted result, or another explicit post-condition. A click or lack of error is not proof by itself.

# Weekly review

Take the owner from a full inbox to zero, one decision at a time. He decides; you prepare.

1. Run `ocean distill --week` (dry run) and show what it would do; on his yes, run it with
   `--yes`. Open the digest it wrote in `01-daily/weekly/`.
2. Walk `ocean memory review list`, oldest first. For each candidate, show its title, source and
   proposed target in two lines, then ask: approve (`ocean memory review approve <id>`, with
   `--type <type>` or `--to <path>` when it has no target), edit, or reject. Never approve
   without his answer.
3. Walk `00-inbox/captures/`: for each capture, file it where its type lives (routing.json),
   turn it into a task or backlog line, or mark it `status: processed`.
4. Run `ocean interests decay` (dry run) and the brief's keep/skip feedback he gives.
5. Finish with `ocean doctor`: report `INBOX_STALE`, `FRONTMATTER_MISSING`, `TYPE_LOCATION`, and
   one next step.

Ask one question at a time. Batch nothing he has not seen.

# Policy — skill observation

Load at a checkpoint, a handoff, or session end (`ocean policy lifecycle`) — never
continuously during a task.

## What counts as a signal

Only these, and only when they actually happened this session:

```
the owner corrected an approach
the same workaround was applied more than once
a skill or capability was invoked and failed
a needed capability did not exist
routing picked the wrong tool, model, or skill for the task
a skill activated when the task did not need it
```

No signal this session ⇒ write nothing. A quiet session produces zero observation lines,
not a summary saying so.

## Where it goes

There is no separate observation log — that would be a second lifecycle subsystem next to
the one that already exists. A signal is recorded exactly like any other durable fact from
the session:

- a corrected approach or a validated judgment call → `ocean policy feedback` territory,
  written to `02-personal/` per that policy's rules
- a missing capability, a bad routing outcome, or a repeated workaround → one line in the
  task's own checkpoint note (`ocean tasks checkpoint <ID> --note "..."`), or the
  session record if there is no task

## What this never does

- **Never rewrites a skill file automatically.** An observation is a candidate for a human
  review, not an edit. Changing a skill, a policy, or a rule file happens through the same
  explicit, reviewed path as any other change to governance — never as a side effect of
  "noticing" something.
- **Never runs as an always-on transcript watcher.** Event-driven only: check at a
  boundary that already exists (checkpoint, handoff, session end), not on every turn.
- **Never generates observation noise.** If the signal cannot be stated in one line with
  the concrete evidence (what was corrected, what failed, what was missing), it is not
  ready to record yet — keep working, revisit at the next boundary.

# Ocean

**One workspace for every AI agent you use.** Ocean is a local-first layer that gives Claude,
Codex, Gemini, Qwen, Cursor, OpenCode and other AI clients the same projects, tasks, memory
and knowledge, on your machine, without a hosted service.

## Why

Every AI client keeps its own memory, its own history and its own idea of what you were doing.
Switch clients and the context is gone. Come back next week and the decisions are buried in a
chat log.

Ocean moves that state out of the clients and into one place you own. Projects, tasks,
decisions and sessions live as plain files in a private workspace on your disk. Every client
reads from and writes to that same workspace through one runtime. A task started in Claude can
be continued in Codex, reviewed in Gemini and closed from the terminal, with nothing explained
twice.

## What it does

- **Projects and tasks.** Each repository you work in maps to a project. Tasks are files that
  declare their own status, so any client can pick one up, checkpoint it and close it.
- **Shared memory.** Durable facts and lessons are curated markdown, indexed for full-text and
  vector search, and served to every client over MCP.
- **Bounded context.** A session gets a small packet of what the work needs, loaded in layers,
  instead of the whole workspace.
- **Client setup.** `ocean clients apply` adds Ocean's MCP server and session hooks to every
  installed AI client, and journals each change so it can be rolled back.
- **Session records.** Shims on your `PATH` record what each AI CLI did, so work can be
  reviewed and resumed.
- **Health checks.** `ocean doctor` reads the workspace, clients and integrations, and names
  the fix for anything broken.

## Principles

- **Local-first.** Records are files on your machine. No account, no server, works offline.
- **The record is the truth.** Boards and indexes are generated from the records and checked
  for drift, never hand-edited.
- **Provider-neutral.** No model is special. The workspace outlives any client.
- **Explicit authority.** Reads are free. Writes outside the workspace need an explicit flag.
- **Public engine, private data.** The engine holds code and templates only. Your records never
  enter it, and Ocean never stores provider credentials.

## Install

Requires Node.js 22.16 or newer, on macOS or Linux.

```bash
npm install --global @amoree-code/ocean
ocean setup
```

The same name is on npm and GitHub Packages. `ocean setup` creates the
private workspace at `~/ocean` (or `OCEAN_ROOT`), adds shims for the AI CLIs and starts a small
background service.

## Quick start

```bash
ocean clients plan               # which AI clients Ocean can connect, and what changes
ocean clients apply --yes        # connect them
cd ~/code/acme && ocean project register   # make this repository a project
ocean tasks new "Add login"      # open a task any client can continue
ocean doctor                     # check that everything is wired
```

## Uninstall

Changed your mind? One command puts the machine back the way it was before Ocean:

```bash
ocean uninstall                  # shows what it would remove; changes nothing
ocean uninstall --yes            # removes it
npm uninstall --global @amoree-code/ocean
```

It removes only what Ocean added: its MCP entries and hooks in every AI client, the skills and
rules it copied into them, the background service, the shell profile line and the shims. Your
own settings and servers stay as they are. Your workspace (memory, tasks, sessions) is kept, so
`ocean setup` reconnects it later; `ocean uninstall --yes --purge` deletes it too, after you type
its folder name.

## This repository

The repository mirrors `~/ocean/`. The engine in [`kernel/`](kernel/) is public and complete.
Every workspace folder ships as an empty `.gitkeep`: its files hold private data and never
leave the machine, and the root `.gitignore` is a whitelist so none can be committed by
accident.

```text
~/ocean/
├── 00-inbox/          intake waiting for triage
├── 01-daily/          daily summaries
├── 02-personal/       durable personal facts
├── 03-professional/   work documents
├── 04-projects/       projects, one folder per category
├── 05-knowledge/      reusable lessons and decisions
├── 06-templates/      templates for tasks, decisions and sessions
├── charter/           rules every AI client loads
├── bridge/            machine-local state: config, profiles, sessions, skills
└── kernel/            the engine: packages/, docs/, scripts/
```

Projects are grouped by who they belong to: `company/`, `personal/`, `freelance/`,
`former-company/`, `vendor/`, and `uncategorized/` for a new one.
`ocean project move <id> <category> --write` files a project.

- **Provider-neutral.** No model is special. Providers are entry points that can be added,
  swapped, or removed; the workspace outlives any of them.
- **Explicit authority.** Reads are free. Writes outside the workspace, promotions and
  installs show a preview and need an explicit flag (`--yes`, `--apply`, `--approve`).
  Nothing is promoted or published implicitly.
- **Verified, not claimed.** A provider saying "done" is not evidence. Completion is an
  independent check passing, and the result records what was verified versus assumed.
- **Public engine, private life.** The engine holds code, tests, and templates only. Your
  records, governance, and machine state live in a separate private workspace and never
  enter it. Ocean never stores provider credentials.

## Requirements

- **Node.js 22.16 or newer** (Ocean uses the built-in `node:sqlite`).
- macOS or Linux. Windows runs the engine and its tests; the layout move and some
  integrations are untested there.
- On Linux, recording a provider's terminal session needs `node-pty`, which has no Linux
  prebuild: npm compiles it when `python3`, `make` and a C++ compiler are present
  (`sudo apt install -y python3 make g++`) and skips it otherwise. Ocean installs and runs either
  way; without it, providers run attached to your terminal and their output is not recorded.
  An npm that blocks install scripts (it prints `npm warn install-scripts`) skips that compile
  even with a toolchain: install with `npm install --global --allow-scripts=node-pty
  @amoree-code/ocean`. macOS needs neither: node-pty ships a prebuild there.
- The AI clients you want to connect, installed and signed in the usual way. Ocean does not
  install credentials and does not need an API key of its own.

## Install

```bash
npm install --global @amoree-code/ocean
ocean setup
```

The npm package is `@amoree-code/ocean` (the name `ocean` belongs to another project); the
command is `ocean`.

The same package and name are on GitHub Packages. The earlier name `@ameer.abdulkareem/ocean`
stops at 1.1.0 and points here.

`ocean setup` creates the private workspace and connects your shell:

- the workspace at **`~/ocean`** — or the directory in `OCEAN_ROOT`, if set;
- shims for the AI CLIs on your `PATH`, so their sessions are recorded;
- a line in your shell profile (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc` or the fish config);
- a login service (a LaunchAgent on macOS, a systemd user unit on Linux, a startup script on
  Windows) that keeps the local runtime running.

It never writes inside the installed package. `ocean setup --help` shows its options. Running
`ocean` with no command starts a short first-run guide; `ocean onboard --status` shows its
steps without running them.

## First useful workflow

```bash
ocean clients plan              # which installed AI clients Ocean can connect, and what changes
ocean clients apply --yes       # add Ocean's MCP server and session hooks to them (journaled)
ocean doctor                    # read-only health check; FAIL lines name the fix
```

Make a folder an Ocean project, then work in it from any connected client or the terminal:

```bash
cd ~/code/acme
ocean project bind acme "$PWD"  # this folder is the project "acme" (records in ~/ocean/04-projects/uncategorized/acme)
ocean project move acme company --write  # file it under ~/ocean/04-projects/company/acme
ocean context                   # what Ocean knows here: project, memory, active tasks
ocean tasks new "Ship the login page"
ocean memory reindex            # build the search index (the background service keeps it current)
ocean memory search "login"
```

A connected client opened in that folder starts with a bounded Ocean context line, can search
and read your records over MCP, and proposes facts worth keeping. `ocean memory review`
approves or rejects them; `ocean clients restore` undoes the last `clients apply`.

## Uninstall

```bash
ocean uninstall                 # shows what it would remove; changes nothing
ocean uninstall --yes           # puts every client config, hook, service and shell line back
npm uninstall --global @amoree-code/ocean
```

It removes only what Ocean wrote: the MCP entries, hooks and native-memory switches from

## MCP

`ocean clients apply --yes` adds Ocean's MCP server to each supported client; `ocean mcp
config` prints the entry for a client you configure by hand. The server is local `stdio`
only and receives no provider credentials. It offers:

- **reads** — `brain_search`, `brain_read`, `brain_neighbors`, `memory_read`,
  `memory_history`, tasks, sessions, handoffs, projects, profiles, `ocean_context`,
  `ocean_status`, `ocean_doctor` and `people_lookup` (a person by exact name or alias);
- **writes** — `memory_write` (only when you ask a client to remember or change something;
  an update must name the record's current hash), `memory_propose` (a candidate for your
  review), `memory_delete` (soft, undone by `memory_restore`), `ocean_handoff_create`, and
  `ocean_session_promote`.

Every call is logged as `{ts, client, tool, ok}` only — never the question or the content —
in `bridge/state/mcp/calls.jsonl`; `ocean clients ledger` summarizes it. See [MCP](docs/mcp.md).

## Agent skills

Ocean ships provider-neutral Agent Skills under `packages/harness/skills/core/`, invoked
by name from any registered client. The core loop:

- `catch-up` — reconstruct project state, completed work, blockers, and the next action.
- `core-thinking` — separate facts from assumptions and choose the smallest valid
  solution before executing.
- `verification` — turn an implementation claim into a focused, repeatable check.
- `session-handoff` — produce a compact continuation packet for the next session.

Alongside them: `business-logic`, `design-thinking`, `graft`, `loop`, and `use-browser`.
See [skills/index.json](packages/harness/skills/index.json) for the current catalog.
`ocean skill learn <completed-session-id>` extracts a candidate skill from a finished
session, and `ocean skill review <candidate-id> promoted` activates it.

Skills reach every client by themselves. At each session start Ocean copies any new or updated
skill — the engine's core skills, and the ones in the skill hub (`bridge/skills/`, where
`ocean market install` puts a skill and where you can make your own) — into Claude, Codex,
Gemini and Hermes. `ocean market install|update` copies at once, and `ocean market uninstall`
removes the copies it made. A copy you edited inside a client after Ocean's version is left as
you wrote it. `ocean skill sync` still does the core skills by hand.

## Public engine, private workspace, machine state

```text
~/ocean/                        private workspace (OCEAN_ROOT) — local only, never published
├── 00-inbox/ … 06-templates/   your records: inbox, daily, personal, professional,
│                               projects, knowledge, templates
├── 07-notes/                   your own notes: agents read them, never write them
├── charter/                    your rules and the policies they route to
└── bridge/                     machine state: sessions, config, client integrations, shims

<npm prefix>/lib/node_modules/@amoree-code/ocean/
                                the engine: code, the empty workspace template, skills
```

Three things are kept apart:

- **The engine** is public and read-only at runtime. It holds no record of yours.
- **The private workspace** holds everything that is yours. `ocean setup` seeds it from an
  empty template; nothing in it is ever copied back into the engine.
- **Machine state** (`bridge/`) is specific to one computer: sessions, client wiring, shims.

Two release gates enforce the boundary. The npm tarball is built by `pnpm release:pack`,
which refuses any workspace folder, machine-local config, credential file, source, test or
source map, any template file beyond its approved empty placeholders, and anything the
privacy scan flags (home paths, e-mail addresses, credential shapes). The source export
(`scripts/publish.mjs`) uses the same deny list. See [Security](docs/security.md).

## Security

- Ocean never stores provider credentials; each client keeps its own login.
- `bridge/` is created owner-only. Secrets do not belong in any Ocean file.
- Text Ocean keeps from a session — summaries, promoted results, handoffs — passes through
  redaction of secret shapes and your home-directory paths first.
- The MCP server is local `stdio` only; nothing listens on the network unless you start
  `ocean gateway` (127.0.0.1, token required).

See [Security](docs/security.md) for the workspace boundary and access control.

## Troubleshooting

- **`ocean: command not found` after install** — npm's global `bin` is not on `PATH`:
  `npm prefix --global` shows the prefix; add its `bin` to `PATH`.
- **`EBADENGINE`, `No such built-in module: node:sqlite` or `does not provide an export named
  'backup'`** — Node is older than 22.16;
  upgrade it and reinstall.
- **The workspace is in the wrong place** — set `OCEAN_ROOT` and run `ocean setup` again.
- **A client does not see Ocean** — run `ocean doctor`, then `ocean clients apply --yes`,
  and restart the client.

More in [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md).

# Architecture

See [operating-model.md](operating-model.md) for the canonical ownership, request-flow,
provenance, credential, CLI/MCP, and provider-boundary contract.

Ocean is a local-first operating layer for AI agents, implemented as a Node.js
runtime for running headless AI agent CLIs (Claude, Codex, Gemini, Antigravity, Hermes)
inside one workspace. The engine repository is public and
provider-neutral; all user data and technical state live in a private workspace next to it.

Capabilities declare the operation, authority, idempotency, and independent verification
contract. Infrastructure implements the mechanics; a provider response never substitutes for
the post-condition check. The reference `workspace.read` capability enforces the profile path
boundary and returns a content hash.

## Adding a capability

1. Propose one narrow operation with its authority, idempotency, and verification contract.
2. Implement provider mechanics under `src/infrastructure/` without adding business rules.
3. Enforce profile/session allowlists and explicit approval for writes.
4. Add denied, timeout, and post-condition tests before exposing the operation through MCP.
5. Record evidence from the independent verification result, not from the provider response.

## Packages

The kernel is a pnpm workspace of seven packages. Each may import only the packages below
it, and nothing may form a cycle — `pnpm check:deps` enforces both (rules in
`.dependency-cruiser.cjs`), plus "application code never imports an infrastructure
concrete" in every package.

| package | holds |
| --- | --- |
| `ocean` (`packages/harness`) | CLI (`src/main.ts`, `src/interfaces/`), composition root, providers, wrappers, process, auth, install, profiles, gateway, scheduler, onboarding |
| `@ocean/services` | browser, Obsidian, workspace doctor, the Ocean and Obsidian MCP servers |
| `@ocean/loop` | tasks, handoff, runs (`runAgent`), loops, sessions, operations, hooks, the SQLite session store |
| `@ocean/context` | context ladder, packet, intent router, resource injection, references, cost |
| `@ocean/brain` | brain index and service, memory, evidence, capture |
| `@ocean/market` | skills (catalog, curation, hub, observer) and MCP connection wiring |
| `@ocean/core` | domain types and ports, and `shared/` — paths, fs-utils, project resolution, task lookup |

The paths below that start with `src/` are inside `packages/harness`.

## Public engine / private workspace boundary

This repository (`engine/`) contains only source, tests, templates, and build output — no
user data. Everything Ocean reads or writes at run time lives in a separate **workspace**
root (see [workspace.md](workspace.md)). The two are joined only through paths resolved at
startup (`packages/core/src/shared/paths.ts`) and are never mixed into the same directory tree or the same git
history.

## Execution flow (`ocean run`)

1. `main.ts` parses the command and calls `runAgent`.
2. `runAgent` loads the named profile (`profile-loader.ts`), opens the session store, and
   creates a `Session` row with status `created`.
3. `runAgent` assembles a lean prompt: context references (the profile's `contextSources` and
   an exact task-id packet record, both filtered by `allowedPaths`), a skill index with SKILL.md paths,
   and a bounded profile facts digest — paths and pointers, not file bodies
   (see [context.md](context.md)).
4. `runProvider` builds the provider's CLI invocation and `runHeadless` spawns it, streaming
   stdout as JSON/text events back into the session's event log.
5. The session status transitions to `running`, then `completed`/`failed` based on exit code.

See [providers.md](providers.md), [profiles.md](profiles.md), [sessions.md](sessions.md),
and [context.md](context.md) for detail on each stage.

# Universal browser client setup

Ocean owns the browser workflow and task format. AI clients connect to the same
browser through a standard MCP server; client-specific setup only changes where
the MCP entry is stored.

## Two ways to reach a browser

| Route | Use it when | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| Marketplace `dev.ocean/chrome-devtools` | The owner's own signed-in Chrome, from every client | `ocean clients apply` writes it |
| Isolated Playwright stack (further down) | A separate profile, not your signed-in Chrome | `ocean mcp playwright-config` |

## Your signed-in Chrome, in every client

```text
AI client -> ocean market exec dev.ocean/chrome-devtools -> ocean-browser-mcp (chrome-devtools-mcp --autoConnect) -> running Chrome
```

Each client starts its own stdio server per session; there is no background service and no
extension. The server is the npm package `ocean-browser-mcp` (source: amoree-code/Ocean-BROWSER-MCP),
which runs Chrome DevTools MCP 1.12.0 pinned exactly, with usage statistics and CrUX off, and
it attaches to the Chrome you already use, with its open tabs and signed-in sessions.

Setup, once:

1. In Chrome, open `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging` and enable the debugging server.
2. `ocean market install dev.ocean/chrome-devtools --yes` (shows the permissions it asks for).
3. `ocean clients apply --yes` adds a `chrome-devtools` entry to every supported client
   (`ocean clients plan` shows what would change first). Restart a client that is open.
4. **Chrome asks to allow each new connection.** Every client session that first uses a browser
   tool raises Chrome's prompt; accept it within 60 seconds or the call times out. A tool that
   times out waiting for the browser is retried by the next call.

`ocean doctor` reports `BROWSER` once the capability is installed: OK when Chrome's debugging
server is listening, WARN when Chrome is closed or the switch is off. A sandboxed shell that
blocks loopback also sees WARN.

**This is full access.** A connected client can read and operate every page Chrome exposes,
including signed-in sites. Page content is untrusted data, and the access does not authorize a
specific action: sending, purchasing, deleting and account or security changes still need your
explicit approval. Any client with the entry has this access; any local process running as you
can start the same server.

**What it covers.** Tabs, navigation, accessibility snapshots, click, fill and forms, file
upload, screenshots, script evaluation, console messages and network requests (32 tools).
`list_pages` lists web pages only: `chrome://` and extension pages are left out, so its count can
be lower than Chrome's tab count. **Downloads:** there is no download tool; a click on a download link downloads to Chrome's own
folder, and `chrome://` pages (the downloads list included) cannot be opened, so confirming a
download needs a client that can read that folder.

**Client limits seen.** Claude Desktop does not negotiate MCP roots, so tools that read or
write files (upload, a screenshot saved to a path) are limited to the OS temp directory there.
Codex, asked a plain question, uses its own computer-use tool instead of the browser tools;
name the tool or ask for "the chrome-devtools tools".

**Recovery.** A client restart starts a new server. Page ids do not survive a reconnect, so
call `list_pages` again before acting on a page.

**Turning it off.** `ocean market uninstall dev.ocean/chrome-devtools`, then `ocean clients
apply --yes` removes the entries; or turn the debugging server off in Chrome to cut access at
once. `ocean clients restore` undoes an apply batch.

The browser bridge (a loopback HTTP endpoint in front of the same server) is retired. On a
machine that installed its service, `ocean mcp browser-service uninstall` removes it.

## Isolated browser stack

```text
AI client -> Playwright MCP -> Chrome/Chromium -> persistent browser profile
```

Use `@playwright/mcp` for the shared browser connection. It supports headed
browser control, structured accessibility snapshots, screenshots, and an
extension mode that attaches to existing Chrome tabs and authenticated sessions.

Add this entry to the client configuration (do not commit credentials or private
profile paths):

```sh

```

```json
  "mcpServers": {
    "playwright": {
```
