## Client-neutral task shape

The shared skill should normalize a request to:

```text
url: <starting URL>
task: <human-readable outcome>
continue: true
verify: <observable success signal>
```

The client plans; Playwright performs the browser actions; the skill requires a
post-condition after each state-changing action and stops when the success signal
is verified. Use Ocean's `ocean browser run` JSON tasks for deterministic,
repeatable workflows and persistent Ocean sessions.

## Client wiring

The same MCP entry works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI,
and other MCP-compatible clients. Only the configuration location differs. A
client skill is optional: MCP provides the tools, while a skill supplies the
prompt and task conventions.

## Safety boundary

Keep profiles scoped to the intended sites. Require human confirmation for
submission, upload, download, purchases, messages, or other consequential
actions. Never configure this workflow to impersonate a user in an assessment
or to bypass a site's rules.

# Browser capability

Ocean exposes a provider-neutral browser capability through the `ocean browser` CLI.
The implementation uses `playwright-core` with an already-installed Chromium-family
browser. Ocean never downloads a browser binary during install or build.

## Lifecycle

```text
ocean browser detect
ocean browser open --profile default
ocean browser show <session-id>
ocean browser events <session-id>
ocean browser close <session-id>
```

`open` launches a headless browser on loopback CDP, persists the browser metadata in
the private `bridge/sessions/sessions.sqlite`, and returns an Ocean session id. Every
later operation reconnects to that session. Browser profiles and downloads stay under
the private workspace `system/browser/` directory.

## Operations

```text
ocean browser navigate <session-id> <url> [--approve]
ocean browser read <session-id>
ocean browser observe <session-id>
ocean browser extract <session-id> <selector> [--attribute <name>]
ocean browser click <session-id> <selector> --expect navigates|stays|count:<selector>:<number>
ocean browser type <session-id> <selector> <text> [--no-clear]
ocean browser select <session-id> <selector> <value>
ocean browser scroll <session-id> [delta-y]
ocean browser wait <session-id> [--selector <selector>] [--url-contains <text>]
ocean browser upload <session-id> <selector> <path>... --approve
ocean browser download <session-id> <selector> [--destination <directory>] --approve
ocean browser submit <session-id> <selector> --approve
ocean browser run <session-id> <task-file> [--approve]
```

Cross-origin navigation and upload/download/submit require explicit `--approve`.
Every operation returns JSON and records only bounded operation metadata in the
session event log; page content, cookies, tokens, and credentials are not persisted.

`type` supports normal form controls, `contenteditable` elements, and editor containers
that expose a nested `textarea` (the pattern used by CodeMirror/Monaco). It focuses the
live editor, replaces its contents with keyboard input, then re-reads the live value.

Task files are JSON with an ordered `steps` array and optional `retries` (capped at 3):

```json
{
  "retries": 1,
  "steps": [
    { "action": "navigate", "url": "https://www.freecodecamp.org/learn/" },
    { "action": "type", "selector": ".monaco-editor", "text": "const answer = 42;" },
    { "action": "click", "selector": "button[type=submit]", "expect": "stays" },
    { "action": "submit", "selector": "button[type=submit]" }
  ]
}
```

The runner stops on the first failed verification. Submit and cross-origin navigation
still require `--approve`.

## Browser availability

Use `OCEAN_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` to select a Chromium-family executable when the
automatic paths are insufficient. The default unit suite uses the fake provider:

```text
pnpm test
```

Run the real Playwright integration check explicitly when a local browser is
available:

```text
OCEAN_BROWSER_INTEGRATION=1 pnpm test
```

The integration test is opt-in and does not run in CI by default.

## Safety and rollback

The browser provider is isolated under `src/infrastructure/providers/`; domain and
application code use only JSON-safe browser types. Downloads sanitize remote filenames
and stay inside their destination directory. Removing the browser CLI, provider files,
tests, and `playwright-core` dependency is the rollback boundary; private runtime data
can be left untouched or removed separately by an explicit owner decision.

# Context

A headless run (`ocean run`, the scheduler, the task loop, the gateway) sends the provider one
prompt assembled by `runAgent` (`packages/loop/src/runs/run-agent.ts`). Every supported provider
is an agentic CLI with file access, so the prompt carries **references, not bodies**: the
provider reads a file only when the request needs it. Formatting lives in
`packages/loop/src/runs/prompt-assembly.ts`; context references in
`packages/context/src/context/context-references.ts`.

## Prompt sections

Non-empty sections are joined with a blank line, in this order:

| Section | Content | Bound |
|---|---|---|
| `request` | the request text | — |
| `profile` | `## Effective Ocean profile` as compact `key: value` lines; empty and default fields are omitted, `writePolicy` is always shown | — |
| `instructions` | `profile.instructions` | — |
| `skills` | `## Ocean skills`: one line per profile skill, `- name: description (path to SKILL.md)`; bodies are not inlined. Owner-reviewed promoted skills matched by the request follow inline, since they have no SKILL.md | description 300 B; promoted skills 4 KB total, a truncated one ends with a marker naming its entry id, `ocean skill list` and the candidate store file (not granted: it also holds unreviewed candidates) |
| `facts` | `## Durable profile facts`: newest first, then a pointer to the full set (`ocean memory facts <profile>` and the store file) | 2 KB including the pointer |
| `handoff` | `## Ocean handoff` with the compact handoff context, verbatim | handoff budget |
| `context` | `## Context references`: `- path (recordType, bytes B): reason` per reference | 4 KB; overflow is listed in the manifest |

## How references are chosen

1. **`profile.contextSources`.** Each entry is resolved against the run's working directory with
   `realpath`, and kept only if its canonical path equals or lies under the canonical path of one
   of `profile.allowedPaths`. An entry that does not resolve, or that escapes through a symlink,
   is recorded in `omitted`. A kept entry is `stat`'d for its size and never opened.
2. **Context packet.** When `profile.memory.enabled`, the request is classified
   (`intent-router.ts`) and, only when it resolves to the exact-record rung of the T-198 ladder
   (`context-ladder.ts`: a task lookup naming one validated id), passed to the context packet
   (`context-packet.ts`), which selects that task's `task.md`. Memory, knowledge and decision
   lookups are not used headlessly: they are keyword-triggered ("memory", "recall", "lesson",
   "best practice"), so they would point ordinary engineering prompts at private records. A
   selected record must also lie inside `profile.allowedPaths` (the same realpath boundary,
   resolved against the run cwd); one that does not is recorded in `omitted`. Unknown or
   low-confidence intents select nothing, and any error (a malformed project-bindings file, for
   example) also fails closed to no references, so a run never fails on a file it would not
   have read.

Paths recorded in events are always relative: to the run cwd for `contextSources`, to the Ocean
root for packet records. Only the prompt, which is persisted as a hash, carries the absolute form.

## Context manifest (`src/domain/context/context.ts`)

```ts
{
  files: string[],                  // referenced contextSources entries
  bytes: number,                    // size of the context-references section
  maxBytes: number,                 // the section cap (4096)
  omitted: string[],                // disallowed, unresolvable or overflow references
  compactedSummary: string | null,  // null
  compression: object | null,       // null: nothing is inlined, so nothing is compressed
  lastContextCheckpoint: string,    // ISO timestamp of this build
  references: {                     // what the prompt points at (defaults to [])
    path: string, base: "cwd" | "ocean-root", recordType: string,
    reason: string, bytes: number | null,
  }[],
}
```

Validated by `validateContextManifest` (Zod). `runAgent` records it as a `context_manifest`
session event before the provider runs (see [sessions.md](sessions.md#events)).

`context_cost` records `bytes` (the whole prompt), `sources`, `handoffId`, `selectedSkills`
and `sections`: the byte size of each section above plus `separators` (2 bytes per join), which
sum exactly to `bytes`.

## Loading phases

Ocean does not scan all sessions, tasks, personal files, daily files, or transcripts at startup:

1. Bootstrap session metadata and the selected profile.
2. Load the requested task or compact handoff, when supplied.
3. Resolve skill paths, the profile facts digest, and context references; no skill or context
   body is read.
4. Read full artifacts only through an explicit CLI or MCP retrieval, or when the provider opens
   a referenced path itself.

`contextCompression` stays in the profile schema and in the profile identity hash, but it has no
effect on headless prompts now that no context body is inlined, and the profile contract does
not mention it. `packages/context/src/context/context-compression.ts` has no production caller; only its
unit tests exercise it.

Read access: the prompt points the provider at files it must be able to open. `runAgent` passes
these directories outside the run cwd as `readDirectories` on the provider request:

- each skill's folder;
- the profile facts store directory (`system/memory/profiles/`), only when the digest left facts
  out; the grant is the directory, so it also covers other profiles' fact files;
- the canonical parent directory of a context reference, only when that directory itself lies
  inside the profile's canonical `allowedPaths`. A single-file `allowedPaths` entry is referenced
  but never widens to its siblings, and a symlinked entry grants its real location, not the
  link's folder.

Claude receives one `--add-dir <dir>` and Gemini one `--include-directories <dir>` per directory,
so their workspace-confined file tools can read them. `--add-dir` applies to one invocation, so
`resumeAgent` rebuilds the same grant for a resumed Claude turn: the skill index again (the
profile identity is unchanged), the facts check against the current store, and the references
read back from the session's `context_manifest` event. A skill or facts lookup that fails at
resume time (a skill removed since the first turn, an unreadable facts file) drops that part of
the grant instead of failing the turn. Codex's read-only sandbox, Hermes and
Kilo read outside the cwd without a grant.
Antigravity (`--sandbox`) and Kimi have no such flag wired and may be unable to open a skill
outside the cwd; the index line still carries the skill's name and description.

## `ocean context cost`

A read-only report of what each interactive client loads on every request before the user types
anything:

```bash
ocean context cost [--json] [--budget <bytes>] [--project <dir>]
```

- Clients: claude, codex, gemini, hermes, cursor, antigravity (the skill roots `ocean skill sync`
  uses) plus a shared `~/.agents` row.
- Always-on bytes = global rules file(s) (Claude and Gemini `@path` imports resolved one level,
  ignoring code) + Claude's per-project `MEMORY.md` for `--project` (default: cwd; keyed by the enclosing git
  repository root, and a linked worktree by its main checkout, as Claude does) + the
  frontmatter of every installed skill. Skill body bytes are reported but not counted.
- Columns: `client | rules | memory | skills | skill-fm | skill-body | always-on | status`
  (`ok`, `OVER` when above `--budget`, default 12288, or `absent`).
- Per-client assumptions (rules file precedence, memory auto-loading, unknown rules locations)
  are printed as notes. Project-level rules files are not measured.
- Output holds only `~/...` display paths, byte counts and fixed notes, never file contents. The
  command exits 0 even when a client is over budget.

# Ocean entry-point contract

Ocean has one full-head execution path and several compatibility boundaries. The
entry point is part of the session evidence; command resolution alone is not proof
of full governance.

## Entry points

### `ocean run`

This is the canonical `full-head` path. Ocean owns the profile, bounded context,
skills, policy, approval contract, session, provider adapter, output events,
evidence, and explicit capture/promotion boundary.

```text
ocean run
  -> profile and policy
  -> bounded context and provider adapter
  -> provider process
  -> session events and evidence
  -> explicit capture or promotion
```

### Native hooks and the `ocean-<command>` wrapper

A plain `claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `agy`, `hermes`, `kilo`, or `kimi` command
runs the provider's own binary. Ocean never installs a shim under a provider's
own name: a same-name shim only works while its directory is first on `PATH`,
so the same command behaved differently per shell. Clients reach Ocean through
their native hooks instead (`ocean hook session-start --client claude|codex|hermes`).

`ocean setup` installs an `ocean-<command>` wrapper per registered provider
(`ocean-claude`, `ocean-codex`, ...). Running it enters `terminal-shim` with
`observed` control. The wrapper records its entry contract, provider resolution, authentication state,
bounded provider output, terminal input when a TTY is available, lifecycle, and
evidence. It does not claim to own provider-native policy or to provide semantic
conversation capture for raw terminal bytes.

Inspect the boundary with:

```bash
ocean client status
ocean client doctor
ocean client doctor /absolute/path/to/native/provider
ocean session show <session-id>
ocean session events <session-id>
```

### Managed interactive session

This is the target `managed-partial` boundary for provider-native interactive
adapters. It must preserve terminal behavior while making input capture,
context transport, approvals, and limitations explicit per provider. It is not
complete merely because a PTY starts successfully.

Start the managed boundary explicitly with:

```bash
ocean client open hermes
ocean client open claude
```

The command owns the PTY and records a `managed-partial` entry contract. The
provider still owns its native authentication and UI behavior; provider-specific
context injection and semantic prompt capture remain capability claims that must
be proven separately.

Every governed entry point runs the shared session closeout when the provider exits. The closeout
writes a bounded human-readable summary under `bridge/sessions/summaries/`, stores only essential
summary metadata in `bridge/sessions/sessions.sqlite`, and may create a bounded handoff draft.
It does not automatically promote conversation content to memory, knowledge, inbox, daily files,
or skills.

### Desktop wrapper

Desktop clients may launch a provider by absolute path and bypass `PATH`. A
desktop integration is governed only when its supported wrapper setting points to
an Ocean shim and a real process inspection verifies the result. Otherwise the
session is `bypass` or `not proven`.

Passing an observed native path to `ocean client doctor` reports the bypass
explicitly; it does not rewrite client configuration or credentials.

## Session contract

Each governed provider session records a `session_entry_contract` event containing:

- `entryPoint`: `ocean-run`, `terminal-shim`, `interactive-managed`, or `desktop-wrapper`.
- `controlLevel`: `full-head`, `managed-partial`, `observed`, or `bypass`.
- `inputCapture`: `semantic`, `bounded-terminal`, or `none`.
- `contextTransport`: the provider-native or environment transport actually used.
- `policyEnforcement`: the policy boundary actually enforced.
- `promotion`: always `explicit-review`; no conversation is promoted automatically.
- `resume`: provider-native resume support or an explicit unsupported result.

## Data ownership

Runtime sessions and bounded events live in the private Ocean session store.
Provider credentials remain provider-owned. Session summaries are not knowledge.
Captures, knowledge, projects, tasks, Obsidian notes, browser actions, and
schedules require their own explicit operation and approval boundary.

## Status language

- `PROVEN`: the exact entry path and behavior were exercised and evidence persisted.
- `NOT PROVEN`: the path exists but the required real behavior was not exercised.
- `BLOCKED BY CLIENT LIMITATION`: the provider account, model, subscription, or native client blocked proof.
- `BYPASS`: the process was launched outside the managed Ocean boundary.

# Ocean MCP connection

Ocean exposes the governed Obsidian tools through one provider-neutral stdio MCP server. Generate the native client configuration with:

```sh
ocean mcp config
```

Copy the returned `mcpServers` object into the MCP configuration of each approved AI client. The same generated entry works for Claude, Codex, Gemini, Hermes, and other clients that support stdio MCP; only the client-owned configuration location differs.

The server also exposes bounded read-only continuity surfaces: `ocean_task_get`,
`ocean_handoffs_list`, `ocean_handoff_get`, `ocean_session_get`, and `ocean_session_events`,
plus the `ocean://handoffs` resource (`ocean://status`, `ocean://profiles` and `ocean://tasks` are
also listed).
The server identifies itself as `ocean` in `initialize` `serverInfo`. Tool and prompt names are `ocean_*`. The generated config entry is keyed `ocean` (`mcpServers.ocean`) — that key is the client-owned identity of an installed entry, so re-running setup never adds a second server. A client still holding an entry under the legacy key from an older release should remove it. Every client receives the same Ocean-owned metadata; provider-native
transcripts and credentials are not copied between clients. The Obsidian vault server is keyed
`ocean-obsidian`; it never takes the `ocean` key, which belongs to the brain server.

## Memory contract (T-296)

`initialize` returns `instructions`: the same memory contract for every client (Ocean is the
memory; search before answering; explicit saves with `memory_write`; inferred or imported facts
with `memory_propose`; never secrets). `ocean_capabilities` reports the contract version and
whether writes are on; `ocean_ping` is a cheap health check.

Not every client shows `instructions` to its model, but every client shows tool descriptions. So
`brain_search`, `memory_propose` and `ocean_context` each open with when to call them (before
answering about the user; when the user states something worth keeping; once at the start of a
conversation without a start line). A fresh install then uses Ocean without the user writing any
prompt or project instructions.

| Tool | Effect |
| ---- | ------ |
| `memory_read` | one record with its `sha256` |
| `memory_history` | audit entries, newest first; ids feed `memory_restore` |
| `memory_write` | `create` (refuses an existing or same-name/same-title record unless `allowSimilar`) or `update` (needs `expectedHash`); the replaced content is kept |
| `memory_propose` | a server-named candidate under `00-inbox/candidates/<date>/`, for review; with `project` and `kind`, filed by Ocean in that project (below) |
| `memory_delete` | soft delete into trash; needs `expectedHash` |
| `memory_restore` | puts back a deleted record or an earlier version |
| `ocean_context` | the bounded start line (256 bytes or less: project bound to `cwd`, operations) for clients without a session-start hook; read-only, no records |
| `ocean_projects_list` | project ids and names |
| `ocean_handoff_create` | a new cross-client handoff on the user's request: summary + next action, 4 KB at most, secrets and home paths redacted, the calling client recorded as provider; never overwrites; read back with `ocean_handoffs_list` / `ocean_handoff_get` |

An approved candidate's write is audited with its original `origin` (`imported` or `inferred`) and
its `candidate` id, not as an explicit save. `brain_search` uses the local embedder when it answers
and full text otherwise (`vector` in the result says which).

### Call ledger (T-307)

Every tool, resource or prompt call appends one line to `bridge/state/mcp/calls.jsonl` (mode 0600):
exactly `{ts, client, tool, ok}`, where `client` is the name the client sent in `initialize` and
`tool` the called tool (`resources/read`, `prompts/get`, or `unknown` for a name the server does
not know). The question, the arguments, the result and any record content are never written. Lines
older than 90 days, and the oldest half past 2 MB, are pruned. `ocean clients ledger` summarizes it
per client and tool; it is how a client's in-app use of Ocean is shown, from Ocean's side. A client's
self-reported name is attribution, not authentication.

Each summary row keeps that raw name and adds `oceanClient` when the name is known (`mcpClients` in
`packages/harness/src/application/clients/registry.ts`), plus `mode` when the client sends one name
per mode. Claude Desktop sends two: its normal chat is `claude-ai` (`mode: chat`) and agent mode is
`local-agent-mode-ocean` (`mode: agent`). Evidence for one mode is not evidence for the other. An
unknown name, such as `codex-mcp-client` until it is identified, stays unattributed.

Writable roots, fixed in `packages/brain/src/memory/memory-paths.ts`: records under
`02-personal/**` and `04-projects/<id>/memory/**` (caller-chosen, `.md`, never an index or
`CONFLICTS.md`); new files under `04-projects/<id>/docs/**`, only through a filed or approved
`doc` proposal (never `memory_write`, never over an existing file); candidates, versions, trash,
the audit log and the client journal (server-named,
under `00-inbox/candidates/` and `bridge/state/`). A symlink or hard link on the way, a path
outside these roots, a known secret shape or more than 32 KB is refused. Errors carry a stable
`error.data.code` (`EXISTS`, `EXISTS_SIMILAR`, `MISSING`, `OUT_OF_ROOT`, `PROTECTED`, `SYMLINK`,
`HARDLINK`, `SECRET`, `CONFLICT`, `TOO_LARGE`, `INVALID`, `WRITES_OFF`).

Nothing is hard-deleted over MCP. `ocean memory purge` (CLI) lists stored copies older than the
retention period and removes them only with `--yes`. `bridge/config/memory.json` holds
`{"mcpWrites": "on" | "off", "retentionDays": 90, "pullAutoApprove": "off" | "on", "proposeAutoApprove": "off" | "project"}`; `mcpWrites: off`
refuses every mutating tool. `pullAutoApprove: on` (default `off`, for a machine whose accounts are
all the owner's) lets `ocean pull --yes` approve what it just proposed through the same write path,
as new records only: a candidate with no target, one that would add to an existing record, a
similar record or a refusal stays for `ocean memory review`; the run's record says which.

### Project filing (T-307)

`memory_propose` with `project` (an id from `ocean_projects_list`) and `kind` lets Ocean, not the
client, choose where a fact made in a project conversation belongs:

| `kind` | Place | With `proposeAutoApprove: project` |
| ------ | ----- | ---------------------------------- |
| `fact` | `04-projects/<id>/memory/<name>.md` | written at once as a new record |
| `doc` | `04-projects/<id>/docs/<name>.md` | written at once as a new file |
| `todo` | none until approved | waits; approval adds one line under `## Open` in `04-projects/backlog.md` |

`name` is lowercase kebab-case (60 characters at most) and required for `fact` and `doc`.
`project` is an Ocean id or a project name in any case (`LetSpeak` finds `letspeak`); the same
goes for `brain_search`'s `project`, which limits a search to that project and global records.

A name Ocean does not know is registered as a project only when it is one of the owner's Claude
projects this machine has seen — names only, read from Claude Desktop's and the browsers' caches
by the always-on service every 15 minutes into `bridge/state/clients/claude-projects.json`
(owner-only), because the caches take tens of seconds to read. It becomes
`04-projects/<slug>/` with `project.json` (`autoRegistered: true`, no paths, tag `claude.ai`)
and the standard layout, never over a folder without a manifest, and `ocean doctor` lists it as
`PROJECT_AUTO_REGISTERED` until the owner keeps it (`autoRegistered: false`), renames or
removes it. Any other name — a topic a client calls a project — stays a candidate. A project
without `project.json`, an existing file, a similar record, a secret or the setting off (the
default) leaves the candidate for `ocean memory review`; the result says `filed`,
`registered` or `review` with the reason. An auto-filed write is audited with its `origin`, its `candidate` and
source `propose-auto-approve`, so `memory_history` shows it. A todo never becomes a task folder:
a task is opened at the owner's request. Project docs are indexed as `project-docs/<id>/…`, in
that project's scope, and `brain_read` takes their workspace path.

The always-on service (`ocean service`) checks every 2 minutes whether the brain index is older
than its files and rebuilds it when it is, so a filed or written record — or a hand edit — is
searchable without `ocean memory reindex`. The new index is built in a temp file and renamed into
place. Vectors come from the local embedder; without it, an index that has vectors waits instead
of losing them, and one without is rebuilt as full text. `OCEAN_NO_AUTO_REINDEX=1` turns it off.

The service stays running: launchd (`KeepAlive`) or systemd restarts it if it exits. After a new
build, `ocean service restart` restarts it without unloading the job (`launchctl kickstart -k`
on macOS). Every session start (`client sync`) checks it and starts an installed service that is
not running; its output says `service: running`, `started`, or `failed` with the command to run.

Tool annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`) are hints for a client's permission UI, not
enforcement: whether a client asks before a call is the client's behaviour and is not assumed.
The server's own checks above are what bound a call.

The server reads the private connection at `OCEAN_ROOT/bridge/integrations/obsidian/connection.json`. It never receives provider credentials. Keep the connection `read-only` until the client route is verified. Mutating tools require both client approval and an explicit `read-write` connection.

## Wiring every client: `ocean clients` (T-296)

`ocean clients detect|plan` lists every AI client and IDE Ocean knows (installed ones, with the
evidence), its tier (`supported`, `context-file`, `unsupported`, `unknown`), the pending change to
its `ocean` entry, its native-memory policy, and the reason or fallback for clients that cannot
connect. `ocean clients apply` prints the plan; `--yes` writes it. Only Ocean-managed entries are
touched: `ocean` (set to `node <current engine> mcp serve`, or to the `ocean` shim with
`mcp serve` when node lives in a version manager's tree — fnm, nvm, volta, asdf, mise, n — so
removing that version does not break every client; each shim falls back from its recorded node to
`node` on PATH, then `/opt/homebrew/bin/node` and `/usr/local/bin/node`), a legacy `ocean` that runs the Obsidian
server (renamed `ocean-obsidian`), and dead entries of the retired atlas gateway. An entry with keys
Ocean does not manage (`env`, headers, a TOML sub-table), a JSON file not in canonical form, or a
YAML list is never rewritten: it becomes a manual step with the exact entry to add.

Each write re-reads the file right before replacing it (a concurrent edit makes Ocean recompute),
keeps the file's mode and writes through a symlink. Rollback uses
`bridge/state/clients/journal.jsonl` (mode 0600): the before/after value of each managed entry
only — never a copy of a client file — and a value that holds a credential shape is kept as a hash,
so restoring it can only remove Ocean's entry. `ocean clients restore [--batch <id>]` undoes an
apply; an entry the user changed since is reported as a conflict and left alone. `ocean clients
repair` (run by `ocean client sync`) re-applies only clients approved by an earlier `apply --yes`.
`ocean clients verify [<id>]` starts each client's configured command and checks it answers as the
brain server — proof the entry launches, not that the app connects. `ocean doctor` fails for an
installed supported client that is not wired or needs a manual edit, warns for an unknown
capability, and reports unsupported clients with their fallback.

The state file `bridge/state/clients/clients.json` records the clients approved by an apply, the
last `ocean clients verify` result of each, and the evidence for each client's use of Ocean:
`ocean clients confirm <id> --label in-app|headless|connected|blocked [--via <evidence>] [--reason
<why>]`. `in-app` means the client's model, in normal use, searched Ocean for a question that named
no tool and cited the record path; it needs `--via` (e.g. the ledger line). `headless` is a scripted
run, `connected` the client's own `mcp list`/`test`; `blocked` needs `--reason` (a login, a missing
app). Only `in-app` makes `ocean doctor` say "checked in the app" (`CLIENT_WIRED`); `blocked` is

`CLIENT_CHECK_PENDING`: a config that launches the server is not proof that the app uses it. Warp
and Xcode are `unsupported` until their MCP support is verified.

`ocean onboard` runs the same plan as its `connect` step: one consolidated review of every detected
client, one confirmation that applies all of them, then `verify` per written client and the in-app
check to do by hand. Without a terminal (or with `--yes`) the step writes nothing and prints the
commands instead. A completed `connect` step reopens on the next `ocean onboard` only when a new,
not yet approved client needs a change; an approved client that drifted is repaired by `ocean
client sync` without asking. `apply` refuses an engine that lives in a temporary directory (a scratch
worktree): every client wired to it would stop starting Ocean once that directory is gone.

Session hooks go through the same plan, apply and restore, for every client whose events are
verified: Claude Code (`~/.claude/settings.json`), Codex (`~/.codex/hooks.json`), Gemini CLI
(`~/.gemini/settings.json`; 0.58 reads the same `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext`), Qwen Code

CLI and Claude Code, whose hook sets `shell: "powershell"` so it behaves the same with or without Git
Bash.

- `ocean memory digest` — at most five lines for `/day-start`: open conflicts, candidates older
  than three days, a stale index, projects without memory records, yesterday's direct writes.

## The memory loop runs in code, not in the model (T-313)

MCP is pull-only: a server offers tools, and the model decides whether to call them. A memory that
depends on the model remembering to read at the start and to save at the end will sometimes do
neither. So Ocean runs both ends of the loop from the client's own hooks, and the tools stay for
what the user asks for explicitly ("remember this", "forget that").

- **Read.** The session-start hook puts the Ocean start line into the session before the first
  message (above). Without a hook, `instructions` and the tool descriptions ask the model to call
  `ocean_context` once.
- **Write.** After a session ends, and before Claude Code compacts one, Ocean reads the client's
  own transcript and captures the durable facts the user stated:
  - Secrets and private paths are replaced (`redactSecrets`) before any text reaches a model. The
    user's newest turns get most of a fixed budget.
  - The model is the session's own client, run read-only through the provider layer: Claude
    (`haiku`) or Codex (its default model). `OCEAN_SESSION_FACTS_MODEL` names another model. The
    call carries `OCEAN_FACTS_CALL=1`, so its own hooks do nothing.
  - Every fact must quote the user's own words. A fact whose quote is not in a user turn is
    dropped: an invented fact, or one taken from the assistant's guess.
  - Each fact becomes a candidate with `origin: inferred` and `source: session:<id>`.
    `approveCandidate` refuses to file such a candidate automatically, whatever
    `proposeAutoApprove` or `pullAutoApprove` say: the owner reviews every one
    (`ocean memory review`). A content-hash ledger keeps one fact from being proposed twice.
  - A per-session cursor (the transcript offset already read, kept as `memory_extract_claim`
    session events) makes a compaction followed by a session end read each turn once. A failed
    model call hands its turns back to the next run.
  - A hook has seconds (Claude Code allows 10, Codex clamps a session-end hook to 3), so the hook
    only starts `ocean hook session-facts` as a detached process. Run it by hand to see what one
    transcript yields:
    `ocean hook session-facts --client claude --session <id> --transcript <path>`.
- **The owner's choice.** `ocean client apply` asks once whether to capture, because it costs one
  small model call per session. `--session-facts on|off` answers without a terminal. Until there is
  an answer, capture is off and `ocean doctor` reports `SESSION_FACTS_UNSET`.
  `ocean memory session-facts [on|off]` shows or changes the answer, and `OCEAN_SESSION_FACTS=on|off`
  overrides it for one process.
- **Quality.** `harness/tests/fixtures/session-facts/` holds conversations with the facts they
  should and should not yield: durable facts, none, an invented quote, a corrected assistant guess,
  a pasted key, and an answer in prose. The tests run them against recorded answers.

### Everything in one view: `ocean mcp status`

```sh
ocean mcp status            # every installed server: how it runs, ready or why not, who sees it
ocean mcp status --check    # also starts each ready server and counts its tools
ocean mcp status --json
```

For each installed server it shows how it runs (npm, pypi, oci, remote), whether it can start
and, if not, why (a missing value, an undeclared permission), each value it takes and where
that comes from (environment, keychain, missing) with the `ocean market secret set` command for
a missing one, the gateway-wired clients that see it, and the clients that get their own entry
for it. Values are never printed. `--check` starts servers for real: a browser server makes
Chrome ask to allow the connection.

### Wiring a client through the gateway

A client reaches installed servers either through one `ocean-gateway` entry or through one
`ocean market exec` entry per server. A machine onboarded fresh (`ocean onboard`, no client
approved yet) starts with the gateway as the default for every client; a machine wired before
keeps per-server entries until its owner switches. The choice lives in
`bridge/state/clients/gateway.json`:

```sh
ocean clients gateway                          # the default and the gateway-wired clients
ocean clients gateway --default gateway        # every client, except those switched off
ocean clients gateway codex off                # one exception, kept across default changes
ocean clients gateway claude-code on
ocean clients plan                             # claude-code: remove <each server>, set ocean-gateway
ocean clients apply --client claude-code --yes
```

That entry runs `ocean mcp gateway --installed-only --client <id>`: every installed server (remote ones
included, which per-server wiring leaves out) through one process, with the runtime scan and the
access rules below. Ocean's own servers stay direct entries (`ocean`, `ocean-obsidian`), so
their tool names, which skills and hooks call, do not change. A gateway entry you added by hand
(`ocean mcp gateway-config`, without `--installed-only`) is yours and is never removed.
`ocean clients gateway` lists the wired clients and `ocean doctor` reports them as `GATEWAY`.

Rollback: `ocean clients gateway claude-code off` then `ocean clients apply`, which puts the
per-server entries back; or `ocean clients restore --batch <id>` to undo one apply exactly.

### Which client sees which server

The gateway knows which client it serves from `--client <id>` in the entry Ocean wrote (an
Ocean client id such as `claude-code`); for a gateway entry added by hand, from the name the
client gives in `initialize` (`clientInfo.name`). Either is logged as `client: <name>`. It
starts only the servers that client may see; a hidden server never runs
and its tools never reach that client. By default a client sees every server except the
sensitive ones: a server that declares a `filesystem.write` permission, or one that drives a
browser (recognised by its name or package: chrome, devtools, playwright, puppeteer, selenium,
webdriver). Allow or deny per client in `bridge/market/gateway-access.json`:

```json
{
  "clients": {
    "claude-code": { "allow": ["dev.ocean/chrome-devtools"] },
    "codex-mcp-client": { "deny": ["io.github.me/files"] }
  }
}
```

Or change one rule from the command line:

```sh
ocean clients allow claude-code dev.ocean/chrome-devtools
ocean clients deny codex io.github.me/files
ocean clients unset codex io.github.me/files
```

`allow` adds sensitive servers (`"*"` for all of them), `deny` removes any server and wins over
`allow`. Installing a sensitive server prints the `allow` command for it. A client with no entry, or one that sends no name, gets the default. Each hidden
server is logged with the reason. The allow list limits what reaches each client's context; it
is not a boundary against another local process, which can start the gateway with any
`--client` it likes. The file is read when the gateway starts; restart the client after editing it.

### Adding a server: from the registry or your own file

```sh
ocean market search github                        # the official MCP registry
ocean market add io.github.github/github-mcp-server        # shows the permissions, installs nothing
ocean market add io.github.github/github-mcp-server --yes  # grants them and installs
ocean market add ./server.json --yes                       # your own server.json
```

`ocean market search` lists matching servers from the official MCP registry
(`registry.modelcontextprotocol.io`; `OCEAN_MCP_REGISTRY` points at a mirror with the same API,
https or loopback), each with how it runs here (npm, pypi, oci or remote) and the values it
needs. Only the search term is sent. `ocean market add` takes a registry name (latest version,
or `--version <v>`) or a path to a `server.json` in the same format. A deleted registry entry is
refused; a deprecated one is installed with a warning. Registry names may carry capitals; the
capability name is the lowercase form.

Ocean writes the server into the owner's index (`bridge/market/ocean-marketplace.json`, payload
under `bridge/market/own/`) with the permissions its launch needs and nothing more: the runner
(`npx`, `uvx`, `docker`) or the remote's host, and every value it is given. It then goes through
the same install as any server: the description scan, consent, the lock. A refused server (scan
finding, no `--yes`, a `dev.ocean` name) is removed from the index again, so it is never
installed and never started. Adding the same server again is a no-op; a changed one is an
update. `ocean market uninstall <name>` removes it.

### Keys and tokens

A server's values are its declared environment variables, every `{placeholder}` in its
arguments or headers (`GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN={token}`, `Bearer {api_key}`), and any
header that is a secret by itself (`Authorization`). Each is a declared `env` permission, shown
at consent. At launch, through the gateway or `ocean market exec`, each is taken from the
environment, then from the secret store. A required value that is missing stops that server
with the command that sets it; an optional one is left out, together with the argument or
header that carries it, so a literal `{token}` is never passed.

```sh
ocean market secret list io.github.github/github-mcp-server    # each value: environment, keychain or missing
ocean market secret set io.github.github/github-mcp-server token   # reads the value from stdin
ocean market secret remove io.github.github/github-mcp-server token
```

The store is the macOS login keychain (service `ocean-mcp`, account `<capability>:<name>`).
`set` reads the value from stdin and passes it to the keychain through stdin too, so it never
appears in shell history, a process list, a file Ocean writes, or a log. On other platforms
there is no store yet; set the variable in the client's environment.

```mermaid
    Hash -->|unchanged| Done[No write]
    Hash -->|changed| Gate{"read-write connection\n+ approval?"}
    Gate -->|no| Conflict["Logged, not written\n(conflict-log.ts)"]
    Gate -->|yes| Write["vault-writer.ts writes the note"]
    Inbox["ocean obsidian inbox promote"] --> Gate
```

# Migration

Ocean provides an explicit, local migration command. Preview the operation with
`ocean migrate`, then apply the idempotent session database migrations with
`ocean migrate --apply`. The command reports SQLite integrity after applying changes.

## SQLite schema

`SessionStore` (`packages/loop/src/infrastructure/persistence/session-store.ts`) creates missing tables
and applies additive column migrations. `ocean migrate --apply` is the explicit upgrade
boundary. Back up `<workspace>/bridge/sessions/sessions.sqlite` before upgrading if you
want a rollback point (see [sessions.md](sessions.md)).

## Profiles

Profile files are plain JSON validated against `profileSchema` (see [profiles.md](profiles.md)).
New optional fields receive schema defaults. A future breaking profile change must ship an
explicit profile migration before the required field is enforced.

## Moving a workspace

Since the workspace root is a private directory (`~/ocean`) whose `kernel/` this repository
is (see [workspace.md](workspace.md)), moving it is a plain filesystem operation: copy the
workspace root (or `bridge/`, `charter/` and the record areas individually) to the new location,
then point `OCEAN_ROOT` at it (or place `kernel/` as its sibling again for the default
resolution). Re-run the platform startup installer (`ocean setup`) if the workspace path
changed, so the OS-level startup entry points at the correct working directory.

# Ocean operating model

Ocean is the canonical local source of truth for project, task, memory, knowledge,
decision, session, and evidence state. Provider clients are entry points and execution
hands; they are not alternate storage owners.

## Ownership

The Ocean root owns the durable state under `personal/`, `projects/`, and `system/`.
The public `engine/` package contains code, tests, and templates only. Private records
must never be written into the engine package or provider-owned memory files. The
unrelated `second-brain` workspace is outside this boundary and is never read, written,
or integrated.

Provider authentication remains provider-owned. Ocean does not broker credentials,
copy them into prompts, persist them in sessions, or write them to logs. Provider
commands receive only the credentials already managed by their installed client.

## Request flow

```text
arbitrary project cwd
  -> provider entry (native hook, shim, or supported adapter)
  -> deterministic intent classification
  -> project and session resolution
  -> confidence and approval checks
  -> metadata-first candidate selection
  -> bounded context packet
  -> exact record read or approval-gated write
  -> independent result and evidence
```

Startup sends identity only. Retrieval happens on demand through the local operation
layer. The operation layer enforces record type, project scope, field allow-lists,
result limits, byte limits, path safety, freshness, and provenance.

## Ambiguous binding

Project resolution returns `bound`, `unbound`, or `ambiguous` with confidence. An
unbound or ambiguous result produces one focused confirmation question. Ocean never
scans broadly or chooses the first matching project. A missing path, git root, project
name, or binding remains unresolved until the user supplies the missing target.

## Provenance

Every returned record carries its source path, record type, freshness, confidence, and
selection reason. The optional declared provenance is normalized to one of:
`fact`, `preference`, `decision`, `lesson`, `proposal`, `temporary-note`, `task`,
`project`, `execution`, or `unknown`.

Corrections are additive evidence. A correction writes a new record with an explicit
`correction_of` reference; it does not silently rewrite or erase historical records.

## CLI and MCP

Simple deterministic reads use the local CLI/application operation path and do not
require an MCP round trip. `ocean operate <request>` classifies the request and executes
only the mapped bounded operation. Writes remain refused unless the caller supplies the
existing explicit approval contract.

MCP is optional. It is an adapter and discovery surface, not the storage layer, source
of truth, or approval authority. A client bypassing the registered hook, shim, or
adapter may operate outside Ocean; Ocean reports the boundary when it can detect it and
does not claim universal enforcement.

## Verification status

Claude, Codex, and Gemini have verified headless invocation paths on the development
machine. Claude has a registered Ocean `SessionStart` hook; direct hook execution and
configuration registration are proven, while invocation and application by a newly
opened live Claude session require a fresh-session check. Providers without a verified
headless contract remain explicitly unsupported or wrapper-only; executable discovery
alone is not compatibility evidence.

# Profiles

A profile is one JSON file describing one agent configuration. `profile.json` is the machine-enforced
contract, including concise instructions and verification commands.

## Storage and loading

Profiles live at `<workspace>/bridge/profiles/<name>.json` (see [workspace.md](workspace.md)).
`loadProfile(name)` (`src/infrastructure/filesystem/profile-loader.ts`) reads and validates the single
canonical JSON file; legacy profile directories are read only for compatibility during migration.

## Schema (`src/domain/profiles/profile.ts`)

```ts
{
  name: string,                                        // non-empty
  description: string,                                  // default ""
  version: string,                                      // non-empty, default "1.0.0"
  provider: "claude" | "codex" | "gemini" | "antigravity" | "hermes" | "kilo" | "kimi",
  model: string,                                        // non-empty
  role: string,                                         // non-empty
  skills: string[],                                      // default core-thinking + verification
  allowedPaths: string[],                                // default []
  allowedCommands: string[],                             // default []
  writePolicy: "none" | "workspace" | "allowed-paths",  // default "none"
  contextSources: string[],                              // default []
  contextCompression: "none" | "ocean-bounded",        // default "none"
  clients: { [client: string]: { enabled: boolean, model?: string, profile?: string,
    home?: string, mode?: string, capabilities: string[], limitations: string[] } },
}
```

Validation is via Zod (`profileSchema` in `profile.ts`, applied by
`validateProfile` in `profile-validator.ts`); an invalid profile throws before an agent run
starts. `description` and `version` are both optional on disk (they default to `""` and
`"1.0.0"`), so profiles written before these fields existed keep loading unchanged.

## Fields in use today

- `provider` and `model` select which provider CLI runs and are passed through to it
  (see [providers.md](providers.md)).
- `contextSources` and `allowedPaths` bound what a headless prompt references — a source path,
  or a task record selected by the context packet, is only referenced (path and size, never its
  body) if it resolves inside one of `allowedPaths` (see [context.md](context.md)).
- `allowedCommands` is checked before a run starts: when non-empty, the selected provider
  command must appear in the list. `writePolicy` is validated at the same boundary;
  `allowed-paths` requires at least one allowed path. Provider processes still need a
  sandbox or client-native write boundary to enforce individual file writes.
- `description` is a free-text summary of what the profile is for; it has no runtime effect.
- `clients` is the provider capability overlay. It does not duplicate role policy: the same role,
  paths, commands, approval, verification, and skills apply to every enabled client. Only the
  selected client's model/home/mode/capabilities/limitations are added to effective context.
- `version` is a human-assigned label for a profile's configuration (bump it when you
  change a profile's fields); it participates in the identity described below.

When `skills` is empty, Ocean selects only `core-thinking` and `verification`. This is the
small default set; expensive or promoted skills remain prompt-matched and owner-reviewed.
`contextCompression` is kept in the schema and the profile identity, but has no effect on
headless prompts (and is not written into the profile contract): context sources are
referenced, not inlined, so there is nothing to compress.

Writable profiles fail closed because direct provider execution cannot enforce file writes.
`writePolicy` is therefore not treated as advisory; an enforcing sandbox must be added before
profiles with write access can run.

## Session reproducibility (`profileIdentity`)

A profile file can be edited after a session has already been created from it, so a
session records more than the profile's name: `profileIdentity(profile)`
(`src/domain/profiles/profile.ts`) hashes every field of a `Profile` (sha256 of a fixed-key
JSON encoding, including `version`) into one deterministic string. `runAgent`
(`packages/loop/src/runs/run-agent.ts`) computes this hash when it creates a session and
stores it as `Session.profileIdentity` (persisted as the `profile_identity` column in
`sessions.sqlite`, see [sessions.md](sessions.md)).

Two profiles with identical fields — including `version` — always produce the same
identity; changing any field, including bumping `version` alone, changes it. This lets a
session be traced back to the exact profile configuration that produced it, independent of
how the profile file on disk has changed since. Sessions created before this field existed
read back with `profileIdentity: ""`.

## Profile vs. project vs. session

These three are easy to conflate because all three can be named on the command line, but
they answer different questions:

- **Profile** (`bridge/profiles/<name>.json`) — *how* an agent runs: provider, model, role,
  skills, and read/write policy. It is configuration, reused across many runs, and owns no
  data of its own.
- **Project** (`04-projects/<name>/`) — *what* the work is about: the tasks, plans, and
  private notes for one piece of work (see the workspace-root layout in
  [workspace.md](workspace.md)). A project has no execution configuration; a profile
  points at paths, it does not define what lives there.
- **Session** (one row in `bridge/sessions/sessions.sqlite`) — *one run*: the record of a single
  agent invocation, which profile (and, via `profileIdentity`, which exact profile
  configuration) produced it, its status, and its transcript of events (see
  [sessions.md](sessions.md)). A session is created fresh every time `ocean run` starts,
  and can be resumed, but it never becomes a profile or a project.

A profile is loaded by name for a run; the run happens against a project's files (via
`cwd`/`allowedPaths`); the result of that run is one session.

## Default profile

`ocean setup` writes `bridge/profiles/default.json` from
`templates/profiles/default.json` if it does not already exist:

```json
{
  "name": "default",
  "description": "General-purpose assistant profile for ad-hoc work across the active workspace.",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "provider": "claude",
  "model": "sonnet",
  "role": "general assistant",
  "skills": [],
  "allowedPaths": ["."],
  "allowedCommands": [],
  "writePolicy": "workspace",
  "contextSources": []
}
```

## Role profiles

`templates/profiles/` also ships public starter templates for three other roles; unlike
`default`, `ocean setup` does not install these automatically — copy the one you need into
`bridge/profiles/<name>.json` under the workspace root:

- **`strategist.json`** — plans and reasons about approach; `writePolicy: "none"`.
- **`developer.json`** — implements and fixes code; `writePolicy: "workspace"`.
- **`reviewer.json`** — reviews changes and reports findings; `writePolicy: "none"`.

The active instances a workspace actually runs with live only at `<workspace
root>/bridge/profiles/<name>.json` — never inside `kernel/`.

The root-level JSON form is canonical. The older directory form with `profile.json` and
`instructions.md` remains read-compatible during migration; it is not a second authority.

## Skill roots

Profile skill names resolve progressively in this order: public `engine/skills/`, private
`bridge/integrations/claude-code/skills/`, then the active project's `skills/` directory under
`04-projects/<project>/skills/`. Each private or project root uses the same `index.json` and
`<category>/<name>/SKILL.md` contract as the public catalog. The first matching name wins and
duplicate profile names are listed once. The prompt carries a skill index (name, description,
SKILL.md path); the provider reads a skill's body on demand. Owner-reviewed promoted skills,
which have no SKILL.md, stay inline up to 4 KB in total. Private and project skill content never belongs in
the public engine repository.

The local Agent Skills validator runs with `pnpm check:skills`. CI runs the same pinned
Node.js script (`scripts/validate-skills.mjs`) and checks every public `SKILL.md` against its
frontmatter, directory name, and `skills/index.json` entry. It is a development check only;
runtime skill loading does not invoke CI tooling.

Completed sessions can produce a bounded, redacted skill candidate with
`ocean skill learn <session-id>`. The candidate is stored privately with its source session
and remains inactive until an owner explicitly runs `ocean skill review <id> promoted`.

## Suggesting a profile for a task (T-296)

`ocean profiles suggest --task <id> [--profile <name>]` reads the task record and applies a fixed
rule table (`packages/core/src/domain/profiles/profile-selection.ts`): the declared `kind` first,
then the title and objective — security → `security-auditor`, review → `reviewer`, tests →
`tester`, delivery → `devops`, research → `researcher`, planning → `strategist`, implementation
→ `developer`. The first matching rule wins; no match, or a profile that is not installed, gives
`default`. `class: high` or `risk: high` adds "verify before completing" to the reason. An
explicit `--profile` always wins. Every selection, suggested or overridden, is appended to
`bridge/state/profiles/selections.jsonl`.

`ocean run --task <id>` without `--profile` uses the suggestion only when
`bridge/config/runtime.json` sets `"autoProfile": true`; otherwise `defaultProfile` applies as
before. The suggestion never widens a run on its own: it names an installed profile, whose own
`writePolicy` and allowed paths still bound what the run may do.

# Providers

Ocean runs agents by shelling out to the provider's own CLI as a headless subprocess. It
does not call any provider API directly and does not store or manage provider credentials —
authentication is entirely the installed CLI's responsibility.

## Supported providers

`HeadlessProvider` (`src/infrastructure/providers/providers.ts`) is one of:

- `claude`
- `codex`
- `gemini`
- `antigravity`
- `hermes`
- `kilo`
- `kimi`

The private workspace may register additional clients for interactive interception. The registered providers
above are headless-capable through provider-specific invocation contracts; the executable smoke check verifies
that all seven command names are available, while authenticated execution still depends on each provider account.

## Requirement

The provider's CLI binary must be on `PATH`:

- `claude`, `codex`, `gemini` are invoked by their own command name.
- `antigravity` is invoked as `agy`.
- `hermes` is invoked by its own command name.
- `kilo` is invoked by its own command name.
- `kimi` is invoked by its own command name.

## Interactive limits

`ocean run` is the full-head path. A plain provider command runs natively and
reaches Ocean only through its own hooks. `ocean-<command>` enters through the
terminal shim with `observed` control: Ocean records the entry contract,
provider resolution, bounded output, terminal input when a TTY is available,
lifecycle, and evidence, but it does not claim provider-native policy control.

Context transport is provider-specific. Hermes currently receives a partial
environment hint; Claude's verified context injection is limited to print mode;
the other provider adapters are proven for headless prompt transport, not for
interactive context injection. `ocean client status` and `ocean session show`
expose the actual entry contract instead of treating every interactive CLI as a
full Ocean head.

If the binary is missing, the spawn fails at run time (surfaced as an `error` session
event); Ocean performs no live verification that a provider is installed or authenticated
before invoking it.

## Invocation shape (`buildProviderInvocation`)

`claude` is not in this table: it runs through the Claude Agent SDK (see
[Claude](#claude-through-the-agent-sdk)).

| Provider | Command | Args |
|---|---|---|
| `codex` | `codex` | `exec --json <prompt>` |
| `gemini` | `gemini` | `--prompt <prompt> --output-format stream-json` |
| `antigravity` | `agy` | `--print <prompt> --output-format stream-json` |
| `hermes` | `hermes` | `-z <prompt>` |
| `kilo` | `kilo` | `run --auto <prompt>` |
| `kimi` | `kimi` | `--prompt <prompt> --print --output-format stream-json` |

Only `claude` currently supports `--resume`; `resumeAgent` in
[sessions.md](sessions.md#cli-usage) rejects resume for any other provider.

## Execution (`runProvider` → `runHeadless`)

`runProvider` builds the invocation and calls `runHeadless`
(`src/infrastructure/process/cli-process.ts`), which:

- Spawns the command with `cwd` set to the agent's working directory and `stdio` set to
  ignore stdin, pipe stdout/stderr.
- Splits stdout into lines; each line is parsed as JSON if possible (emitted as a `"json"`
  event) or kept as raw text (emitted as a `"text"` event) and forwarded to `onEvent`.
- Applies a timeout (default 60,000 ms); on timeout the process is sent `SIGTERM` and the
  result reports exit code `124`.
- Resolves with `{ exitCode, events, stderr }` once the process closes.

### Claude through the Agent SDK

`runProvider` hands a `claude` request to `runClaudeSdk`
(`src/infrastructure/providers/claude-sdk.ts`), which runs it with the Claude Agent SDK
(`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`, pinned exactly). `claudeSdkOptions` maps the request onto
SDK options, and the SDK turns those into Claude Code's own flags and speaks its stream
protocol:

| Request | SDK option | Claude Code flag |
|---|---|---|
| `resumeId` | `resume` | `--resume` |
| `model` (unless provider-managed) | `model` | `--model` |
| `readOnly` | `permissionMode: "plan"`, `extraArgs.restricted` | `--permission-mode plan --restricted` |
| `readDirectories` | `additionalDirectories` | `--add-dir` (one per directory) |

The contract matches the other providers:

- **Executable:** the SDK runs the user's installed `claude`, resolved past Ocean's shims. The
  SDK's bundled platform binaries are excluded at install (`ignoredOptionalDependencies` in
  `pnpm-workspace.yaml`).
- **Process:** Ocean spawns it through `spawnClaudeCodeProcess`, so `onSpawn` gets its pid and
  its environment is this process's plus the plan's variables.
- **System prompt and settings:** Claude Code's own system prompt (`systemPrompt` preset
  `claude_code`), as `claude -p` has it; left unset, the SDK would send an empty one. Settings
  and `CLAUDE.md` load from every source, as with the CLI.
- **Events:** every SDK message becomes a `"json"` event.
- **Limits:** the run's timeout ends it with exit code `124`, and its output budget (raw stdout
  and stderr bytes, counted as they arrive) with `125`. Both stop Claude's whole process group,
  so a tool subprocess can't hold the run open.
- **Signals:** a Ctrl+C or kill of Ocean is passed on to that group. A process ended by a signal
  is a failed run.
- **Load cost:** the SDK loads only when Claude actually runs.

Provider-side session ids are captured opportunistically: if a `"json"` event's data
contains a `session_id` field, `agent-run.ts` stores it as the session's `providerSessionId`
for later resume.

`discoverProviderCapabilities()` checks whether the selected CLI is installed and returns its
headless, resume, streaming, structured-output, and CLI-managed authentication contract.
`assertProviderCapability()` fails clearly before an unsupported operation. One session uses
one selected provider; Ocean does not silently fall back to another provider.

# Publishing the engine

This page covers the public source export. The npm package has its own guide,
[release.md](release.md); both use the same hard deny list.

The engine is published to a public repository by `scripts/publish.mjs`. Nothing is copied by
hand, and a private file cannot reach the public repository by accident: the export is
deny-by-default and every export is scanned before anything is sent.

## What gets exported

1. **Source.** The content committed at `HEAD` — never the working tree, so an uncommitted edit
   cannot leak and the manifest hash names a real commit.
2. **Hard deny list**, compiled into the script, beats everything: the private workspace
   directories (`brain/`, `charter/`, `bridge/`, `sessions/`, `.index/`, `00-inbox/` …
   `06-templates/`),
   `.git/`, `node_modules/`, `.env*` (except `.env.example`), keys and certificates,
   `credentials.json`, `secrets.json`, `.netrc`, `.npmrc`, `.mcp.json`. Matching is
   case-insensitive. The workspace directories are anchored to the repository root, so
   `packages/brain/` is engine code and stays publishable; machine-local tool config
   (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.gemini/`, `.aws/`, `.ssh/`, `.gnupg/`) is denied at any depth.
3. **`PUBLIC` allowlist.** A file ships only if a line in `PUBLIC` matches it. A file that is not
   listed stays private. A symlink or submodule in the allowlisted set aborts the run.

## Dry run (the default)

```bash
node scripts/publish.mjs            # scratch export + gates + manifest, sends nothing
node scripts/publish.mjs --keep     # also print and keep the scratch directory to inspect it
```

The manifest lists `files`, `denied` (allowlisted paths the deny list blocked), `unlisted` (a
count), the `head` commit, whether the tree is `dirty`, and a content `sha256`.

### Gates

On the scratch export, in order, stopping at the first failure:

| Gate | Tool | Notes |
| ---- | ---- | ----- |
| `gitleaks` | `gitleaks dir` (>= 8.19) | Pinned to a trusted config outside the export; `gitleaks:allow` comments and an exported `.gitleaksignore` are ignored. |
| `trufflehog` | `trufflehog filesystem` | `--no-verification` (a found credential is never sent to its provider), `--no-ignore-tag`. |
| `privacy` | `pnpm check:privacy` | Credential patterns, real private paths, personal data. |
| `template` | `scripts/check-template-purity.mjs` | The shipped workspace template matches its manifest classes (generic defaults, empty private files); an export without the template passes. Not skippable. |

A scanner that is not installed **fails** the run. `--skip gitleaks,trufflehog` skips the
external scanners for a local dry run and marks the result `complete: false`; the `privacy`
gate cannot be skipped. Point at a scanner outside `PATH` with `OCEAN_PUBLISH_GITLEAKS` /
`OCEAN_PUBLISH_TRUFFLEHOG`. Scanner output is never printed — only the verdict, and for the
privacy gate the paths and finding types.

A failed gate names each finding as `{rule, file, line}`, relative to the export. The matched
text is never printed.

### Known limits

- gitleaks' default configuration skips some paths and binary file types (for example images and
  lockfiles). The other two gates are independent layers, but a secret hidden in a skipped file
  type can still pass all three; `PUBLIC` is the control that keeps such files out.
- The scanners find credentials and private paths by pattern. They do not know what is
  private in a sentence. The allowlist is deliberately narrow for that reason.

## Pushing

Pushing is deliberate and bound to what you reviewed:

```bash
node scripts/publish.mjs                                   # 1. review; note the manifest sha256
node scripts/publish.mjs --push --remote <url> --confirm <sha256>   # 2. publish exactly that
```

- `--remote` (or `OCEAN_PUBLISH_REMOTE`) is an `https://`, `ssh://` or `user@host:path` URL. It
  is **never `origin`** and never the source repository itself, whether spelled with a port,
  `.git`, another case, a symlinked path, or an alias that `url.<base>.insteadOf` rewrites to it.
- `--confirm` must equal the manifest hash of the same `HEAD`; otherwise nothing is sent. The
  error does not repeat the hash: it comes from the dry run you reviewed.
- `--push` runs from `main` only (the merged, reviewed tree; a feature branch or a detached
  `HEAD` is refused) and refuses `--skip`, a dirty tracked tree, and any gate failure. These
  checks run before the scanners.
- The commit is made verbatim: no line-ending conversion, filter or attribute from your git
  config or from the exported `.gitattributes` can change the bytes that were scanned.
- The commit **author** is your `user.name` / `user.email` from the source repository, and it
  becomes public in the history; the push result prints it. Check it before the first push.
- The public history is one squashed commit per publish, `publish: <head>`, added on top of the
  public `main` as a plain fast-forward. Nothing is forced or rewritten; when the content is
  unchanged nothing is pushed.
- A credential embedded in the URL is stripped from all output.

## Pre-commit hook

`lefthook.yml` runs `scripts/gitleaks-staged.mjs` on every commit. It warns and continues when
`gitleaks` is not installed — the publish gate above is the fail-closed one.

## Public repository setup (owner steps)

These change the public repository's settings or name and are done by the owner, not by the
script:

1. Create (or rename to) the public repository and add its URL as the publish `--remote`.
2. Protect its default branch: require a pull request, require review from Code Owners
   (`.github/CODEOWNERS`), forbid force pushes and deletions. Allow the publisher to push, or
   publish through a pull request branch instead.
3. Renaming the public GitHub repository is a separate, outward-facing step.

# Releasing the npm package

Ocean ships as **`@amoree-code/ocean`** to both npm and GitHub Packages (the name `ocean` belongs
to another project); the installed command is `ocean`. Up to 1.1.0 the npm name was
`@ameer.abdulkareem/ocean`, now deprecated in favour of this one.

**Releases are automatic (T-312).** Every push to `main` runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`:

1. `scripts/auto-release.mjs` reads what is pending: the root `CHANGELOG.md`'s Unreleased lines
   and any changesets in `.changeset/`. Major on a `major` changeset or a `type!:` line
   (`feat!: …`), minor on a `minor` changeset or a `feat` line, otherwise patch. Nothing
   pending, no release. A version already set by hand and not yet tagged ships as it is.
2. It sets the version in every `packages/*/package.json`, regenerates the marketplace index,
   moves the Unreleased lines under `## <version> (<date>)` in `CHANGELOG.md`, adds
   `## <version>` to `packages/harness/CHANGELOG.md`, and deletes the consumed changesets.
3. The gates run on exactly that tree (`check:skills`, `build`, `check:package`, `test`); only
   then does github-actions commit `chore(release): v<version>`, tag it and push to `main`.
4. The publish job (environment `production`) packs the tag, writes the GitHub release from the
   package changelog section, publishes to npm through **trusted publishing** (OIDC: no token
   is stored anywhere) with provenance, and to GitHub Packages with the job's own token. Each
   step skips what already exists, so a failed publish is fixed by re-running that job.

Nobody publishes by hand. npm trusts only `release.yml` in environment `production` of
`amoree-code/ocean` (`npm trust list @amoree-code/ocean`).

The sections below are what the workflow does, for reading or for checking a tarball locally.

## What the package is

The CLI is `packages/harness`. Its six internal packages (`@ocean/core`, `market`, `brain`,
`context`, `loop`, `services`) are workspace dependencies that are not on npm, so the release
tarball carries them as `bundleDependencies`: each one's built JavaScript sits in the
tarball's `node_modules/@ocean/`, and their third-party dependencies are lifted into the
CLI's own `dependencies`, where npm installs them. Only JavaScript ships — no `src/`, tests,
`.d.ts` or source maps.

## 1. Gates

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm test
pnpm check
```

## 2. Pack

```bash
pnpm release:pack                         # build, then pack into a new temp directory
node scripts/pack-release.mjs --out <dir> # pack an existing build into <dir>
```

It prints the tarball path, file count and sizes. Before the tarball is written,
`scripts/release-boundary.mjs` judges npm's own list of what it would pack, and the pack stops
on any finding:

- the entry point (`dist/main.js`), `templates/`, `skills/`, `market/`,
  `ocean-marketplace.json` and every bundled package must be present;
